1.2.05-103.comment: Before you change lanes to overtake, you need to check your mirrors and do a shoulder check to make sure you're not putting following traffic at risk. Only then can you signal and move over. During the overtaking process, you also need to make sure you don't block oncoming traffic. Just because the car in front is signaling right doesn't mean you should overtake.

1.2.05-104.question_text: How should you end an overtaking maneuver?

options.text: Re-enter the right lane as soon as possible without hindering the vehicle being overtaken
Signal your re-entry clearly and in good time
Switch back to the right lane right in front of the vehicle being overtaken

1.2.05-104.comment: As the overtaking vehicle, you should move back to the right lane as soon as you can. But don't cut in too closely in front of the vehicle you just overtook, as that could hinder or endanger them. Make sure to use your turn signal before you move back in.

1.2.05-105.question_text: What are the speed rules during an overtaking maneuver?

options.text: The overtaking vehicle must be significantly faster
The maximum speed limit must not be exceeded
The vehicle being overtaken must not increase its speed

1.2.05-105.comment: You can only overtake a vehicle in front of you if you're going at least 20 km/h faster than it. Also, remember not to exceed the speed limit while overtaking. The vehicle being overtaken must maintain its speed during the maneuver.

1.2.05-106.question_text: How should you behave when being overtaken?

options.text: Drive as far to the right as possible
Don't increase your speed
Increase your speed

1.2.05-106.comment: When you're being overtaken, try to stay as far to the right as you can to avoid endangering oncoming traffic and the overtaking vehicle. You shouldn't increase your speed during the overtaking process, as that could make it unsafe.

1.2.05-107.question_text: On which side should you overtake a tram that is in the middle of the road (not a one-way street)?

options.text: Right
Left
Left only if other vehicles block the right side

1.2.05-107.comment: Trams should generally be overtaken on the right. If parked vehicles are blocking the right side, you need to stay behind the tram. If the tracks are too far to the right, you can overtake the tram on the left.

1.2.05-108.question_text: When can you overtake a tram on the left?

options.text: In one-way streets
When the tracks are too far to the right
When the right side of the road (not a one-way street) is blocked by other vehicles

1.2.05-108.comment: You should generally only overtake trams on the right. However, you can overtake on the left if the tracks are too far to the right or if the tram is in a one-way street. Just having vehicles blocking the right side isn't a valid reason to overtake on the left.

1.2.05-109.question_text: Which vehicles should be overtaken with a particularly large side distance?

options.text: Bicycles
Motorcycles
Trams

1.2.05-109.comment: When overtaking, you always need to keep a safe distance from other road users. This distance should be particularly large for motorcycles and bicycles, as these one-wheeled vehicles can be less stable and may wobble. The minimum side distance to two-wheeled vehicles is 1.5 meters.

1.2.05-110.question_text: When do you need to signal?

options.text: Before changing lanes to overtake or pass
Before re-entering after overtaking
When leaving a bending right-of-way road straight ahead

1.2.05-110.comment: You need to signal whenever you're changing lanes or turning. This also applies when following a bending right-of-way, but not when you're leaving the right-of-way road straight ahead. And remember, even when signaling, always check that you're not endangering anyone when moving in or out.

1.2.05-116.question_text: You're driving a slower vehicle on a country road. How can you let faster vehicles overtake you?

options.text: - onto the shoulder
- onto the parking lane
- into a pull-off area

1.2.05-116.comment: To let faster vehicles overtake you on a country road, you can move onto a suitable shoulder, a parking lane, or into a pull-off area. You can also slow down or even stop at a suitable spot.

1.2.05-119.question_text: How can you tell that a horse-drawn carriage wants to change direction?

options.text: By the driver extending their arm
By the displayed signaling paddle
By the activated turn signal

1.2.05-119.comment: You can tell that a horse-drawn carriage wants to change direction by one of the following signals: the driver extends their arm, the carriage displays a turn signal, or the driver uses a signaling paddle.

1.2.05-120.question_text: You want to overtake a horse-drawn carriage on a country road. How do you behave?

options.text: - make little noise
- keep a large distance
- high engine speed

1.2.05-120.comment: Drive at a safe speed and pass the horses with as much distance as possible. The animals might get startled by sudden loud noises like a horn or high engine speed and could bolt. So, avoid noise and getting too close.

1.2.05-123.question_text: You want to overtake a horse-drawn carriage on a country road. What’s the right way to behave?

options.text: I pay attention to the driver's hand signals
I keep a safe distance when merging back
I keep as little distance as possible

1.2.05-123.comment: When overtaking a carriage, you need to watch for hand signals from the driver, as they may give you special instructions. Always overtake carriages with a large safety distance to avoid startling the horse.

1.2.05-124.question_text: What distance must you keep when overtaking pedestrians and cyclists?

options.text: - at least 1.5 m in built-up areas
- at least 2.0 m outside built-up areas
- at least 1.0 m in built-up areas

1.2.05-124.comment: To protect cyclists and pedestrians, you must keep a distance of at least 1.5 meters in built-up areas and at least 2 meters outside built-up areas.

1.2.05-125-M.question_text: What do you need to consider when overtaking cyclists in this situation?

options.text: Due to the incline, the cyclists are swerving
I must overtake with at least 1.5 m distance
I must overtake with at least 1.0 m distance

1.2.05-125-M.comment: You need to keep at least 1.5 meters of distance when overtaking cyclists in built-up areas. Because cyclists might swerve, a larger minimum distance is recommended.

1.2.05-126-M.question_text: How should you behave in this situation?

options.text: I stay behind the cyclist
I overtake the cyclist with enough distance
I must let the pedestrian cross the road

1.2.05-126-M.comment: The lane marking is solid, so overtaking is not allowed here.

1.2.06-001.question_text: Which vehicle must wait when a construction site blocks half the road?

options.text: The vehicle on the side of the construction site
The vehicle on the free side of the road
Always the smaller vehicle

1.2.06-001.comment: If you want to pass a parked car or a barrier on your side of the road, you must give way to oncoming traffic, regardless of the size of the vehicles.

options.text: - if you can see that no oncoming traffic is coming
- to not hold up possible oncoming traffic
- since possible oncoming traffic must already wait

1.2.06-006.comment: Your view is blocked by the van, and you can't see if any vehicles are coming towards you. Before proceeding, you need to make sure that no oncoming traffic is approaching. You must wait since the construction site is on your lane.

1.2.06-101-M.question_text: How should you behave in this situation?

options.text: I wait until the oncoming vehicle has passed
I drive in front of the oncoming vehicle
I communicate with the oncoming vehicle about who goes first

1.2.06-101-M.comment: You wait until the oncoming vehicle has passed because the obstacle is on your side of the road.

1.2.07-001.question_text: What must you do if you want to change lanes?

options.text: Announce the lane change in good time
Watch the traffic behind you
Always brake hard before changing lanes

1.2.07-001.comment: Use your turn signal and make sure you’re not endangering other road users before changing lanes. Don’t brake abruptly. If there are vehicles in the lane you want to switch to, wait for a big enough gap in traffic.

1.2.07-105-M.question_text: How should you behave in this situation?

options.text: I’ll switch to the right lane in about 200 meters
I can overtake vehicles in the right lane
I’ll switch to the right lane now

1.2.07-105-M.comment: You should drive as close to the obstacle as possible and only switch to the right lane in about 200 meters. You can overtake any vehicles that are in the right lane.

1.2.07-113.question_text: On a road with multiple lanes in one direction, one lane is ending. How should you behave on the continuing lane?

options.text: Let the vehicles that are blocked from continuing merge using the zipper method
Drive past the vehicles that are blocked from continuing
Make eye contact and decide based on the situation

1.2.07-113.comment: You need to allow the driver of the vehicle on the ending lane to safely merge into the adjacent lane. It's required that vehicles from the ending lane and those on the continuing lane alternate merging right before the lane narrows. This is called the zipper method.

1.2.07-116.question_text: You want to turn right at the intersection. How should you behave correctly?

options.text: I’ll skip the right turn and stay in my lane
I’ll steer sharply to the right to create a gap in the right lane
I’ll wait until all vehicles have passed and then switch to the right lane

1.2.07-116.comment: You should switch to the right lane, which is blocked by waiting vehicles. By waiting, you would block other road users in your lane. So it's better to skip the turn here.

1.2.09-016.question_text: You want to turn left. When should you pay attention to following traffic?

options.text: Before merging
Before turning
After turning

1.2.09-016.comment: When turning left, you should pay attention to following traffic before turning and before merging.

1.2.09-017.question_text: Two vehicles are approaching each other at an intersection. Both want to turn left. In which exceptional case must they turn one after the other?

options.text: If traffic conditions require it
If the design of the intersection requires it
If a junction of equal priority is being used

1.2.09-017.comment: Generally, vehicles turn left in front of each other. However, if traffic conditions or the design of the intersection, like road markings, require it, they must turn one after the other.

1.2.09-018.question_text: Two vehicles are approaching each other at an intersection. Both want to turn left. How should the two drivers behave in general?

options.text: Turn in front of each other
Turn one after the other
Communicate about the type of turn

1.2.09-018.comment: Generally, vehicles turn left in front of each other.

1.2.09-019-M.question_text: You want to turn left. Which driving line should you follow?

options.text: The right driving line
The left driving line
Both driving lines are possible

1.2.09-019-M.comment: You should use the right driving line. The left driving line is meant for oncoming traffic.

1.2.09-101.question_text: What can lead to particularly dangerous situations when turning left in multiple lanes?

options.text: Going too fast
Changing lanes while turning
Strictly following the lane

1.2.09-101.comment: Drive at a moderate speed in multi-lane turning situations. If you go too fast, you might drift out of your lane and into the lane of parallel vehicles. Avoid changing lanes during this turning situation, as there's a risk that a vehicle is in your blind spot right behind you.

1.2.09-103-B.question_text: All three vehicles want to turn left. Who has positioned themselves correctly?

options.text: The yellow car
The truck
The green car

1.2.09-103-B.comment: Only the yellow car has positioned itself correctly. It passed to the right of the traffic island as indicated by the sign 'pass on the right' to then position itself as far left as possible to prepare for the left turn. The green car is incorrectly positioned on the tracks; the truck can only go straight or turn right in this situation.

1.2.09-104-B.question_text: After turning left, you want to turn right immediately. How do you position yourself?

options.text: - red car
- green car
- blue car

1.2.09-104-B.comment: If you want to turn right right after turning left, position yourself in the right lane if there are two lanes for turning left. Otherwise, stay as far right as possible. This way, you can turn right without blocking other road users.

1.2.09-107-B.question_text: Who needs to signal a change of direction?

options.text: The motorcycle
Myself
No one

1.2.09-107-B.comment: The person changing direction must signal it, regardless of the road's importance. So, the motorcycle rider must signal when following the bend in the right-of-way road. If you're going straight, you don't need to signal.

1.2.09-109.question_text: You're in a roundabout. What should you keep in mind?

options.text: You may only drive over a central island if unavoidable due to vehicle size
Stopping in the roundabout is prohibited
You must signal when leaving the roundabout

1.2.09-109.comment: You can only stop in a roundabout if it's unavoidable due to traffic, like in a jam. Signal when you want to leave the roundabout. You should only drive over paved or asphalted central islands if it's absolutely necessary due to your vehicle size. Always give way to cyclists on your right who are staying in the roundabout.

1.2.09-111.question_text: In which situation is turning around particularly dangerous?

options.text: Before hills
Before curves
In fog

1.2.09-111.comment: Turning around can be dangerous in poor visibility (like fog). The same goes for turning in curves and before hills.

options.text: Myself
The blue truck
The red car

1.2.09-112-M.comment: You must always signal when changing direction. Staying on a bending right-of-way road also requires signaling. So, the blue truck must signal. You, as the left turner, also need to signal.

1.2.09-113-M.question_text: Who needs to signal the change of direction here?

options.text: Myself
The red car
The motorcycle

1.2.09-113-M.comment: You should always signal a change of direction early. All three drivers intend to turn, so all three vehicles need to signal.

1.2.09-117.question_text: In which cases do you need to signal a change of direction?

options.text: Before turning into an intersection or property
When I want to follow the bend of a right-of-way road
When I want to leave a bending right-of-way road straight

1.2.09-117.comment: You should always use your turn signal whenever your direction changes. This usually happens when turning onto another road, like when following a bending right-of-way road or turning into an intersection or property.

1.2.09-119.question_text: Why do you have to wait now?

options.text: - cyclist
- green vehicle
- red vehicle

1.2.09-119.comment: When turning, you must let vehicles from the opposite direction pass, including cyclists. The red car has to wait until the green car and the cyclist go by.

1.2.09-120.question_text: You want to turn left. In what order do you prepare for the turn?

options.text: Watch for following traffic, signal direction, position
Signal direction, position, watch for following traffic
Position, signal direction, watch for following traffic

1.2.09-120.comment: When you want to turn left, prepare in this order: 1. look, 2. signal, 3. position. Looking means checking the following traffic in your mirror and with a shoulder check. Then, signal for the left turn. Only when you can ensure you won't endanger other road users should you position yourself for the left turn.

options.text: I must stop at the stop line
I must let the cyclist pass
I may turn before the cyclist

1.2.09-121.comment: You must always stop at the sign "Stop! Give way!" (commonly known as a stop sign). There's usually a stop line. Your wheels must come to a complete stop. Cross traffic has the right of way - next is the cyclist on the opposite side. As a left turner, you must give way to them.

1.2.09-123.question_text: You want to turn left. Who do you have to give way to?

options.text: Oncoming cyclists
Oncoming motor vehicles
Pedestrians wanting to cross the street I'm turning into

1.2.09-123.comment: Traffic coming towards you when you're turning left always has the right of way. This includes cyclists, who also need to be given way. If pedestrians are crossing the street you're turning into, they have the right of way too.

1.2.09-124.question_text: You want to turn left. What difficulties can arise?

options.text: Visibility issues from oncoming traffic
Misunderstandings with oncoming left turners
Left turners can come dangerously close

1.2.09-124.comment: When turning left, vehicles coming towards each other need to turn in front of each other (tangential turning). This can lead to poor visibility of straight-moving traffic. Especially with left-turning trucks, visibility can be severely blocked, making wide turns (turning behind each other) safer. Misunderstandings can occur between drivers if one wants to turn behind and the other wants to turn tangentially.

1.2.09-125.question_text: Why do you have to stop now?

options.text: Because of the tram
Because of the cyclist
Because of the white car

1.2.09-125.comment: You're on a priority road, so you have the right of way over the white car coming from the right. However, as a turning vehicle, you must yield to straight-moving traffic, in this case, the tram. You need to stop.

options.text: - don't overtake before the level crossing
- now overtake with enough side distance
- overtake before the level crossing as soon as the cyclist is gone

1.2.09-126.comment: You can't overtake the moped before the level crossing. Generally, no vehicles should be overtaken from the level crossing sign with a post to the tracks.

1.2.09-127.question_text: Why do you have to brake now?

options.text: Because of the motorcycle
Because of the van
Because of the female cyclist

1.2.09-127.comment: The motorcyclist is coming at high speed from the left. He probably hasn't seen you because of the oncoming vehicle. Even though you have the right of way, you need to brake to avoid an accident.

1.2.09-128-M.question_text: Why do you have to wait before turning right?

options.text: Because of the female pedestrian
Because of the female cyclist
Because of the black car

1.2.09-128-M.comment: When you want to turn, you have to give way to road users going straight. In this case, you need to yield to both the female pedestrian and the female cyclist and allow them to cross safely.

1.2.09-129.question_text: What do you need to pay attention to here?

options.text: - keep braking
- give way to the car
- signal when leaving the roundabout

1.2.09-129.comment: Since the blue car is already in the roundabout, you must yield to it and brake. You only need to signal when leaving the roundabout.

1.2.09-131-M.question_text: The cyclist wants to go straight. How should you behave here?

options.text: I stay behind the cyclist
I overtake the cyclist

1.2.09-131-M.comment: Vehicles that want to turn must let bicycles that are going straight on or next to the road pass before turning. It doesn't matter if the bikes are motorized or not.

1.2.09-132-M.question_text: Why do you have to wait to turn here?

options.text: Because of the motorcycle
Because of the truck
Because of the female pedestrian

1.2.09-132-M.comment: Here you need to pay attention to the turning rules. Wait because of the truck and the motorcycle before you turn.

1.2.09-133-M.question_text: Who needs to signal in this situation?

options.text: Me
The blue car
The red car

1.2.09-133-M.comment: You and the blue car are changing direction, so you both need to signal your turn.

options.text: I slow down
I stay in the right lane for now
I switch to the left lane immediately

1.2.09-134-M.comment: The motorcycle behind you has already switched to the left lane and will pass you on the left. To merge into the left turn lane in time, you need to slow down.

options.text: Because of the yellow car
Because of the red vehicle
Because of the green car

1.2.09-135-M.comment: At an intersection, straight-going vehicles have the right of way. You need to wait to turn until the yellow car has crossed the intersection.

1.2.09-136-M.question_text: What should you expect in this situation?

options.text: The blue car is going straight
The red bus will start moving immediately
The pedestrian will wait

1.2.09-136-M.comment: The blue car is passing the stopped bus and might continue straight, even though it's in the turning lane. Since you're turning left, it has the right of way.

1.2.09-137-M.question_text: Why do you need to stop now?

options.text: Because of the electric scooter
Because of the pedestrians
Because of the tram

1.2.09-137-M.comment: There's an electric scooter in your blind spot, so you need to stop to avoid putting it in danger.

options.text: I let the cyclist pass
I check my right shoulder
I turn before the electric scooter

1.2.09-138-M.comment: Straight traffic always has priority, whether the cyclist is on the road or a bike path. To make sure no other cyclists are approaching, you need to check your right shoulder.

1.2.10-005.question_text: You're coming from a street with a lowered curb and want to turn into another street. A car is coming from the left. What applies here?

options.text: Anyone entering a street from a lowered curb must yield
The 'right before left' rule
The lowered curb doesn't matter for yielding

1.2.10-005.comment: When coming from a lowered curb (common in residential areas), the 'right before left' rule doesn't apply. You must wait until you can enter the road without endangering other road users, who have the right of way.

1.2.10-101.question_text: How should you behave when starting from the side of the road?

options.text: Watch for traffic from behind
Signal
Just looking in the rearview mirror is enough

1.2.10-101.comment: If you're merging into traffic from the side of the road, you need to signal your intention. A glance in the rearview mirror and over your shoulder is necessary to merge safely, keeping in mind that you must yield to oncoming traffic.

1.2.10-104.question_text: You want to enter a street from a traffic-calmed area. How should you behave?

options.text: Let pedestrians pass on the sidewalk
Signal before turning
Observe the 'right before left' rule

1.2.10-104.comment: When entering a street from a traffic-calmed area, you must yield to other road users. The 'right before left' rule doesn't apply here! Signal before turning and pay special attention to cyclists and pedestrians.

1.2.10-105.question_text: You want to enter a street from a traffic-calmed area. Cyclists are coming from the left. Who must wait?

options.text: I must wait
The cyclists must wait
Everyone must stop and communicate

1.2.10-105.comment: When entering a street from a traffic-calmed area, the 'right before left' rule is suspended. You must yield to pedestrians, cyclists, and vehicles in flowing traffic.

1.2.10-106.question_text: You're trying to turn right from a property onto a street. Cyclists are coming from the left. Who has to wait?

options.text: I have to wait
The cyclists have to wait
Everyone has to stop and communicate

1.2.10-106.comment: When leaving a property, you generally have to wait and give right of way to all other road users. This includes pedestrians on the sidewalk and cyclists. Be especially careful here.

1.2.10-107.question_text: You're trying to turn from a property onto the road over the sidewalk. What do you need to pay attention to?

options.text: Road users on the sidewalk must not be endangered
You may need to direct traffic
Always pay attention to the flowing traffic first

1.2.10-107.comment: When turning from a property over the sidewalk onto the road, you must give way to pedestrians on the sidewalk, cyclists on bike paths, and vehicles in flowing traffic. You must not endanger any other road users. If in doubt, you should have someone help you merge into traffic.

1.2.10-108.question_text: You're trying to exit a property. What's correct?

options.text: I have to wait until pedestrians have crossed the exit
I can go if pedestrians give up their right of way
I honk briefly to make pedestrians let me out

1.2.10-108.comment: When exiting a property, you must yield to all road users, including pedestrians and cyclists. If a road user gives up their right of way, you can go, as long as you don't endanger anyone.

1.2.10-109.question_text: You want to back out of a parking space into flowing traffic. How should you behave?

options.text: I must not endanger flowing traffic
I must signal before starting
I must watch the traffic behind me

1.2.10-109.comment: When backing out, you must not endanger other road users. Use your turn signal to show that you want to enter the road. Check your rearview and side mirrors, and do a shoulder check to make sure there are no cyclists in your blind spot.

1.2.11-003.question_text: In slow-moving traffic, certain areas must be kept clear. Which ones are these?

options.text: Intersections
Railway crossings
Property exits

1.2.11-003.comment: In slow-moving traffic, you must keep areas clear for emergency vehicles, such as intersections, railway crossings, and pedestrian crossings. This rule doesn't apply to property exits. If you notice someone wanting to enter the road from their property, you should let them merge into traffic.

1.2.11-006.question_text: Which areas in the road traffic space must be kept clear in slow-moving traffic?

options.text: Intersections
Pedestrian crossings
Bus stops

1.2.11-006.comment: Pedestrian crossings (like 'zebra crossings') are meant to allow pedestrians to cross the road safely. Therefore, you must keep pedestrian crossings clear at all times. If you enter an intersection (or junction) in slow-moving traffic, you risk blocking cross traffic or making oncoming left-turning vehicles wait unnecessarily. This would cause even more congestion and hinder traffic more than needed.

1.2.11-103-M.question_text: You want to go straight ahead. How should you behave correctly?

options.text: I stay in my lane
I switch to the right when there's enough space
I overtake the vehicle next to me and change lanes

1.2.11-103-M.comment: The car in front of you is blocking your lane. However, you shouldn't overtake on the right before the intersection, as that would be too dangerous. Keep your distance, reduce your speed, and stop if necessary. Continue straight when the lane is clear and the traffic light is green. You can only switch to the right if there's a sufficiently large gap in traffic.

options.text: Wait before turning left and keep the central island clear
Turn smoothly to avoid blocking those behind
First wait in the central island where the other car is standing

1.2.11-104.comment: If tram tracks run through the left-turn lane and you want to turn left when a tram is approaching, you should wait with enough distance before the tram tracks. Once the tram has passed, you can turn left.

options.text: Slow down
Speed up
Swerve left

1.2.11-105.comment: If a cyclist in front of you is about to swerve left, you must not overtake them if the road is narrow and there's oncoming traffic. You wouldn't be able to maintain a safe distance of 1.5 to 2 meters.

1.2.11-108.question_text: In which cases are you not allowed to enter an intersection, even if the light is green?

options.text: If I have to wait at the intersection because traffic is jammed
If a police officer signals me to stop
If there’s a sign saying 'Stop. Yield.' at the intersection

1.2.11-108.comment: You can't enter an intersection even with a green light if traffic is jammed, as intersections need to stay clear for emergency vehicles. Also, if a police officer is directing traffic, their instructions take priority over traffic lights. Generally, a green light means 'go', but other traffic signs that regulate right of way still apply.

1.2.11-110-M.question_text: Why do you need to slow down and be ready to brake here?

options.text: - for the cyclist
- for the green vehicle
- for the pedestrian

1.2.11-110-M.comment: You don't need to slow down for the pedestrian since they're far enough from the narrow spot. The red vehicle is stopped, so there's no need to brake for it either. However, you should reduce your speed for the cyclist, as they might suddenly switch to the road and create a dangerous situation.

1.2.11-111.question_text: Why do you need to keep braking?

options.text: - for the garbage truck
- for the blue truck
- for the cyclist

1.2.11-111.comment: The blue truck is facing a garbage truck coming towards it, which forces it to stop. Since the garbage truck might swing into your lane while turning, you need to wait until it's properly positioned. The cyclist isn’t a reason to brake.

1.2.11-112.question_text: You want to go straight. How should you behave?

options.text: - at the stop line
- between the yellow and blue vehicle
- directly behind the yellow vehicle

1.2.11-112.comment: In stop-and-go traffic, you can’t block an intersection or entry point, even with a green light or right of way. You might need to wait at the stop line and can only move forward when the vehicles ahead are far enough away.

1.2.11-114-M.question_text: When are you allowed to turn?

options.text: Only when the truck driver clearly signals he’s yielding his right of way
Only if I don’t endanger or significantly hinder cross traffic
Immediately, since the truck driver is signaling me to go

1.2.11-114-M.comment: Since you want to turn left, oncoming traffic has the right of way. You can only proceed when the truck driver clearly signals that he's yielding, while still being mindful of cross traffic. Just flashing your lights isn’t enough.

options.text: At railway crossings
At narrow and unclear road sections
Directly behind pedestrian crossings

1.2.12-001.comment:
Stopping means a vehicle is halted for less than 3 minutes for non-traffic reasons, without the driver leaving. If the driver stays longer or leaves, it’s considered parking. You can’t stop everywhere to avoid endangering other road users. Prohibited areas include:
- No stopping zones
- Railway crossings due to the risk of collision with a train
- Narrow and unclear spots with less than 3 meters of clearance
- Unclear curves
- Hilltops
- Pedestrian crossings and the area before them (at least 5 meters away), but not after.

options.text: At the roadside if it prevents the use of marked parking spaces
On right-of-way roads outside built-up areas
On right-of-way roads within built-up areas

1.2.12-002.comment: Once you stop your vehicle for more than three minutes for non-traffic reasons, it’s considered parking. This isn’t allowed everywhere. You can’t park in areas marked as no stopping or parking zones, or where you block other road users. Parking is also prohibited on right-of-way roads outside built-up areas. Use side strips or parking bays.

options.text: On the roadway if there’s a suitable shoulder on the right
On marked lanes with directional arrows
At taxi stands

1.2.12-103.comment:
You can only stop where you don’t endanger other road users. This is the case on a shoulder separated from the roadway by a continuous white line. You can’t stop:
- on marked lanes meant for merging
- on the roadway if there’s a shoulder
- at bus stops or other public transport stops
- at taxi stands, to avoid blocking access for taxis
- on highways or main roads, even on the shoulder
Watch out for cyclists!

options.text: On pedestrian crossings and up to 5 meters before them
Directly behind pedestrian crossings
Over manhole covers

1.2.12-104.comment: You can’t stop on or up to five meters before a pedestrian crossing, as this obstructs the view for other road users, making it harder to see pedestrians. After a pedestrian crossing, you can stop. Stopping is allowed on manhole covers, but parking is not.

options.text: At the roadside if it prevents the use of marked parking spaces
In front of lowered curbs
Directly behind pedestrian crossings

1.2.12-105.comment: You can’t park at the roadside where you block marked parking spaces and hinder other road users. Parking is also prohibited in front of lowered curbs, which help wheelchair users cross the street. It’s safe and allowed to park after a pedestrian crossing.

1.2.12-106.question_text: Where can you park on the left side in the direction of travel?

options.text: In one-way streets
Where tracks are laid on the right side
Where parking is prohibited on the right

1.2.12-106.comment: You can only park in the direction of travel on the right side of the road. This applies even if all parking spaces are on the left. You may need to turn around if it's allowed. The only exception is one-way streets, where you can park on the left. If there are tracks on the right, you must also park on the left, but always pay attention to parking bans.

options.text: Someone who stops for more than three minutes
Someone who leaves their vehicle
Someone who waits longer than three minutes at a closed railway barrier

1.2.12-107.comment: If a driver intentionally stops their vehicle and stays there for more than three minutes or leaves the stopped vehicle, that counts as parking. Stopping and waiting at a barrier doesn't count as parking, regardless of time, because it's due to traffic conditions.

1.2.12-108.question_text: What is the minimum distance you must keep when stopping or parking in front of a pedestrian crossing?
1.2.12-108.comment: There's a strict no stopping or parking rule on a pedestrian crossing and up to 5 meters before it. This way, you as a driver can see the crossing clearly, and pedestrians have a good view of the traffic.

1.2.12-110.question_text: How far must you park away from a railway crossing with a warning sign?
1.2.12-110.comment: At a railway crossing with a warning sign, the train has the right of way. So, you can't block the view of the crossing, and there needs to be enough space for waiting vehicles in case of a traffic jam caused by the train.

1.2.12-111.question_text: If you want to park in a town in front of a railway crossing, what distance must you keep?
1.2.12-111.comment: At a railway crossing with a warning sign, the train has the right of way. To avoid blocking the view of the tracks, you need to keep a safety distance of 5 meters.

1.2.12-112.question_text: How far before and behind a bus stop sign are you not allowed to park?
1.2.12-112.comment: There's a parking ban of 15 meters before and behind the bus stop sign to allow public transport to easily pull up to and leave the stop.

1.2.12-113.question_text: At bus stops, you can only stop if buses aren't hindered. How long can you stop there at most?
1.2.12-113.comment: You can only stop for a maximum of 3 minutes. If a vehicle is not moved for more than 3 minutes, it's considered parked. So, stopping for up to 3 minutes is allowed.

options.text: The white car
The dark car
Neither car

1.2.12-121-M.comment: The zigzag line marking indicates a parking ban. If there's no marking on the road, there's a parking ban of up to 15 meters before and behind the bus stop sign. In this case, the white car is parked incorrectly because it's on the marking. The dark car is parked correctly.

1.2.12-122.question_text: When are you not allowed to park in the right lane?

options.text: If there's a properly paved shoulder next to the lane
If there are tracks on the lane
If there's a suitable parking lane next to the lane

1.2.12-122.comment: In general, parking is prohibited if it could hinder or endanger other road users. This includes visibility issues. Parking is also not allowed if there are parking options away from the lane, like on the shoulder or in marked parking spaces. If you park in the lane anyway, you might get fined for 'double parking'. So, parking is not allowed in all three situations.

1.2.12-123-M.question_text: What should you pay attention to here?

options.text: You can't stop left of the road marking
Slow vehicles should drive on the shoulder as much as possible
The road marking must never be crossed

1.2.12-123-M.comment: Never stop left of the road marking. You would hinder or even seriously endanger following vehicles. The shoulder here is meant for parked, stopped, and slow vehicles. If you're driving slowly, you should use a sufficiently wide and well-paved shoulder. In this case, you can cross the thick solid line that marks the official road boundary with your vehicle.

1.2.12-124.question_text: Which vehicles are allowed to stop in the second lane?

options.text: All taxis when picking up or dropping off passengers
All vehicles when loading or unloading
All vehicles when the hazard lights are on

1.2.12-124.comment: In the second lane, only taxis can stop in special cases when passengers are getting in or out.

options.text: On merging and diverging lanes
On marked lanes with direction arrows
In front of driveways to properties

1.2.12-125.comment: You can't stop on merging or diverging lanes. You also can't stop on lanes marked with direction arrows, except for driveways to properties.

options.text: The red car
The yellow car
Both cars

1.2.12-126-M.comment: Stopping is not allowed at pedestrian crossings and within five meters before them. This rule ensures clear visibility for approaching vehicles and pedestrians wanting to cross.

options.text: - on the left and right side strips
- only on the left side strip
- only on the right side strip

1.2.12-128-M.comment: In one-way streets, you can only drive in one direction. If there are side strips on both sides, you can park on either side.

1.2.12-131.question_text: You're looking for a parking spot on the right side of the road. There's no bike lane next to your lane. How many meters before and after an intersection can't you park?
1.2.12-131.comment: To avoid blocking visibility, you can't park 5 meters before and after an intersection.

options.text: In front of fire department access points
In all one-way streets
In no-parking zones

1.2.12-132.comment: Stopping means a vehicle is halted for less than 3 minutes for non-traffic reasons while the driver stays inside. If the driver leaves or stops longer, it's considered parking. You can't stop everywhere to avoid endangering other road users. This includes fire department access points and no-parking zones, where stopping and parking are treated differently. This doesn't apply to all one-way streets.

1.2.12-133.question_text: You're looking for a parking spot on the right side of the road. There's a bike lane next to the road. How many meters before an intersection or junction can't you park?
1.2.12-133.comment: To avoid blocking visibility, you can't park 8 meters before and after an intersection or junction.

1.2.16-002.question_text: How should you behave when you see a vehicle with hazard lights on?

options.text: I reduce my speed
I prepare for sudden dangers
I continue driving at the same speed

1.2.16-002.comment: Hazard lights can mean many things. To be safe, you should reduce your speed and be especially careful when passing the vehicle.

1.2.16-101.question_text: For what purpose can the horn be used outside of built-up areas?

options.text: As a warning signal
As an overtaking signal
As a call signal

1.2.16-101.comment: You can use the horn to signal your intention to overtake outside of built-up areas. You can also use it to warn others of dangers. However, using the horn without a specific danger, like as a call signal, is not allowed.

1.2.16-102.question_text: For what purpose can the horn be used in built-up areas?

options.text: As a warning signal
As an overtaking signal
As a call signal

1.2.16-102.comment: In built-up areas, the horn can only be used as a warning signal in case of danger. Using the horn to greet someone or as an overtaking signal is not allowed, as it would create unnecessary noise. You can only use the horn or headlights to signal an overtaking maneuver outside of built-up areas.

1.2.16-103.question_text: What should you do if you break down in a tunnel?

options.text: Turn on your hazard lights
Park your vehicle in a breakdown bay if possible
Leave the engine running as a precaution

1.2.16-103.comment: In a tunnel, there's not much room for other vehicles to get around. So, if you break down, try to stop in one of the marked breakdown bays. Turn on your hazard lights and turn off the engine because of the high risk of poisoning from exhaust fumes in the tunnel.

1.2.16-104.question_text: You're approaching a traffic jam in a tunnel. What should you do?

options.text: Turn on your hazard lights
Turn around and leave the tunnel
Turn off the engine and leave the vehicle at the end of the jam

1.2.16-104.comment: If you see a traffic jam ahead, it's important to turn on your hazard lights right away to warn drivers behind you. This helps them react better. While you're stuck in traffic, you should turn off the engine but not leave the car. Turning around in a tunnel is not allowed.

1.2.17-001.question_text: What do you need to pay attention to regarding your vehicle's lighting?

options.text: They must be properly installed
They must be clean
They must be functional

1.2.17-001.comment: You need to make sure your vehicle's lights are properly installed. Besides being fully functional, the lights should also be clean so that other road users can see you, even in bad weather or in a tunnel.

1.2.17-102.question_text: How can you prevent oncoming traffic from being blinded by your low beam headlights?

options.text: Adjust the beam according to the vehicle's load
Only use approved bulbs for each headlight
Check the alignment after any repair to the headlights

1.2.17-102.comment: To avoid blinding oncoming traffic, make sure your low beam headlights are properly adjusted, and that you check their alignment after repairs or replacements. If you need to change the bulbs, only use approved ones.

1.2.19-002.question_text: When must you stop before a railway crossing?

options.text: When the red light starts flashing
When the barriers start to lower
When a railway worker waves a white-red-white flag

1.2.19-002.comment: All road users must stop and wait at a railway crossing when the red light is flashing, when the barriers are lowering, when the barriers are down, or when a railway worker is waving a white-red-white flag. You must wait until the crossing is clear.

1.2.19-004.question_text: A railway worker is waving a red light at a railway crossing. What does this mean?

options.text: You must wait before the railway crossing
You may cross the tracks carefully
The red light has no significance for you

1.2.19-004.comment: All drivers and other road users must wait at a safe distance before the crossing when a railway worker is securing a little-used crossing with a red light. Waving the red light means that the tracks are closed and trains have priority.

1.2.19-008.question_text: At the entrance to an industrial area, there's a stop sign with the addition 'Industrial Area, trains have priority'. What do you need to keep in mind?

options.text: Approach railway crossings at a moderate speed
Trains have priority at all railway crossings
Motor vehicles have priority at railway crossings without a stop sign

1.2.19-008.comment: Even if there are no barriers or stop signs at the railway crossings in the entire industrial area, drivers must give way to all trains. Always expect a train, watch the tracks closely, and approach the tracks at a moderate speed.

1.2.19-101.question_text: You're driving on a forest road and approaching a railway crossing without a stop sign. What should you do?

options.text: Approach at a moderate speed and watch for any trains
Listen for whistles or bells indicating a train is coming
Drive through without stopping, as trains must yield here

1.2.19-101.comment: Even without a stop sign, drivers must yield to trains at field and forest road crossings. Approach the crossing at a moderate speed and listen for any approaching trains. Watch the tracks and stop if necessary to let the train pass.

1.2.19-102.question_text: How should you behave at a railway crossing where the barriers are closed?

options.text: Wait before the stop sign, keep intersections clear
Turn on your parking lights in the dark
Use the traffic space, wait close to the barrier

1.2.19-102.comment: At a railway crossing with closed barriers, all drivers must wait before the stop sign. If there are no traffic signs, keep a safe distance from the tracks. Make sure you don't block intersections or entrances while waiting. In the dark, your lights must be on, and parking lights are enough.

1.2.19-104.question_text: When can you cross an unbarriered railway crossing with flashing lights after a train has passed?

options.text: When the red flashing light is off
Immediately after the train passes, even if the red light is still on
As soon as oncoming traffic starts, even if the red light is still on

1.2.19-104.comment: You can only cross the railway crossing after the red flashing light has turned off, as another train might follow. Don't let oncoming traffic tempt you to go if the waiting driver there starts moving too early after the train has passed.

1.2.19-105.question_text: You're approaching a barriered railway crossing. Where should you wait if you get stuck on the crossing due to traffic?

options.text: Before the stop sign
Right before the tracks
At the barrier

1.2.19-105.comment: If you can't cross the railway crossing quickly due to traffic, you should stop before the stop sign. Stopping right before the tracks or at the barrier is not allowed, as you could be hit by the train or trapped by the barriers.

1.2.19-107.question_text: At a railway crossing in the city, the barrier is closed. Where should you wait?

options.text: Before the stop sign
Before the last marker
Before the first marker

1.2.19-107.comment: Trucks and vehicles with trailers (over 7.5 tons total weight) only need to wait after the single marker outside of built-up areas. Inside the city, they must wait before the stop sign.

1.2.19-109.question_text: What does this traffic sign mean?

options.text: Indicates existing overhead electric lines
Rail traffic always has priority
You must always wait when a rail vehicle approaches

1.2.19-109.comment: The stop sign indicates that rail traffic has priority here. You must wait before the crossing when a rail vehicle is approaching. A flashing arrow in the stop sign indicates overhead electric lines, which is important for oversized transports.

1.2.19-110.question_text: Before a railway crossing, there's a red light signal from a road merging from the right without a stop sign. Where should you wait?

options.text: At the stop line
If there's no stop line, before the light signal
I can move up to the railway crossing after observing traffic

1.2.19-110.comment: When there's a red light signal, you must stop. To avoid blocking traffic from the merging road on the right, the red light signal is placed several meters away from the actual crossing. Wait at the stop line or at the light signal if there's no line.

1.2.19-111.question_text: How should you behave in this situation?

options.text: - stop before the stop sign
- pass left of the safety post
- pass right of the safety post

1.2.19-111.comment: The railway employee is securing the crossing, so you should stop before the stop sign.

1.2.19-112.question_text: Who must wait at a stop sign with a red flashing light in the shape of an arrow pointing right?

options.text: Right turners
Straight drivers
Left turners

1.2.19-112.comment: A stop sign with a red flashing arrow pointing right is found after a crossing or junction following a railway crossing. The right arrow signals that drivers turning right must wait.

1.2.19-113.question_text: What does this combination of traffic signs indicate?

options.text: - that I can approach here at a maximum of 10 km/h
- that I can cross at a maximum of 10 km/h
- that rail vehicles can only travel at 10 km/h

1.2.19-113.comment: This combination of traffic signs indicates a railway crossing. Drivers may only approach the crossing at 10 km/h and can also cross at that maximum speed.

options.text: I wait before the stop sign
I carefully cross the tracks
I wait on the tracks

1.2.19-114.comment: If there's a risk that you might stop on the tracks due to a traffic jam or slow traffic, stay before the stop sign and wait until you can cross the railway crossing without stopping. Fatal accidents can happen if a car stuck on the tracks can't move out of the way of an approaching train.

1.2.19-115.question_text: You're approaching a railway crossing. The barrier is starting to lower. What should you do?

options.text: I wait before the level crossing
I continue if no train is in sight
I turn on the hazard lights

1.2.19-115.comment: When you're approaching a railway barrier that's lowering, you must wait before the crossing. This applies even if no train is visible yet. You don't need to turn on your hazard lights.

1.2.19-116.question_text: Where should you expect unprotected railway crossings?

options.text: On lightly traveled roads
In industrial and port areas
On field and forest paths

1.2.19-116.comment: You should expect unprotected railway crossings (without barriers or signals) in industrial and port areas, on field and forest paths, and on lightly traveled roads.

1.2.20-004.question_text: Which vehicles must you allow to depart from marked bus stops?

options.text: Regular buses
School buses
Taxis

1.2.20-004.comment: You must let regular and school buses leave marked bus stops if they signal their intention to depart, like by using their turn signal. Taxis are an exception since they aren't bound to fixed stops or schedules.

1.2.20-103.question_text: You want to pass a regular bus that has stopped at a bus stop. What should you keep in mind?

options.text: - pass with enough side distance
- pass carefully
- watch for oncoming traffic

1.2.20-103.comment: It's allowed to pass a regular bus that is stopped at a bus stop. You will likely enter the oncoming traffic lane while passing, so pay special attention to oncoming traffic. It's wrong to pass too closely to the bus, as this could endanger any pedestrians stepping out. You don't need to go at walking speed, but be especially careful.

1.2.20-107-M.question_text: How should you behave correctly in this situation?

options.text: I stay behind the tram
I drive past the tram on the right
I overtake the tram on the left

1.2.20-107-M.comment: As a driver, you must be considerate of public transport and its passengers. In this situation, where the tram is stopped and people at the stop need to cross the road to board, you should stop behind the tram and wait until all passengers have boarded or disembarked.

1.2.20-108-M.question_text: How should you behave in this situation?

options.text: I keep my speed
I drive with increased attention
I slow down to walking speed now

1.2.20-108-M.comment: Since passengers might step onto the road unexpectedly, you should increase your attention. However, you can maintain your speed.

1.2.22-101.question_text: How far can a load stick out behind the reflectors without needing a marking?
1.2.22-101.comment: The lights or brake lights indicate the end of the vehicle. You should use this when estimating the safety distance. If an object is sticking out from the vehicle in front, it should be visually marked and stick out at least one meter. You should factor this into your safety distance and increase it accordingly.

1.2.22-102.question_text: How should a load that sticks out more than 1 meter beyond the vehicle's reflectors be marked at night?

options.text: With a red light and red reflector
With an orange warning sign
By turning on the fog light

1.2.22-102.comment: If you're transporting a load that sticks out more than 1 meter beyond the vehicle, it must be marked with a red light and a red reflector. This makes the end of the load visible to other drivers, allowing them to maintain a safe distance. An orange warning sign indicates the transport of hazardous goods. The fog light doesn't improve visibility and shouldn't be used.

1.2.22-104.question_text: What can happen with just a 20% overload?

options.text: Overloading the brakes
Worsening of steering behavior
Damage to load-bearing vehicle parts

1.2.22-104.comment: The entire vehicle design, driving behavior, and center of gravity of a car are tested and calibrated by the manufacturer for a certain maximum load limit. Exceeding this limit can negatively affect the vehicle's handling. Additionally, you risk permanent damage like bending or breaking load-bearing parts of your car.

1.2.22-106.question_text: What do orange warning signs on a vehicle mean?

options.text: - Hazardous goods transport
- Livestock transport
- Transport of perishable food

1.2.22-106.comment: An orange warning sign indicates that a vehicle is carrying hazardous goods, warning other drivers. In case of an accident, the orange sign helps rescue services identify the situation.

1.2.22-107.question_text: What should you consider when transporting a load?

options.text: - not to be obstructed
- not to shift even during a hard brake
- never to stick out over the front of the vehicle

1.2.22-107.comment: You need to secure the load carefully to prevent it from falling. The driver shouldn't be obstructed by the load, including visibility. You must follow the allowed dimensions and weight limits. The load can only stick out forward by a maximum of 50 cm if it's above a height of 2.5 m. This rule helps reduce injury risk in a rear-end collision.

1.2.22-108.question_text: At what height can a load stick out up to 50 cm in front of your vehicle?
1.2.22-108.comment: If your vehicle is up to 2.5 m high, the load can stick out 50 cm in front. This extension is also allowed for trailers and must not be exceeded to minimize injury risk in rear-end accidents.

1.2.22-109.question_text: What must you consider when loading your vehicle?

options.text: My vehicle must not exceed the allowed axle loads
I must secure the load against shifting with suitable means
My vehicle can exceed the total weight limit by a maximum of 5%

1.2.22-109.comment: When loading your vehicle, you must not exceed the allowed axle loads. You need to secure the load according to recognized technical standards.

1.2.23-001.question_text: Who is responsible for the roadworthy condition of a registered vehicle?

options.text: The driver
The owner
The liability insurance

1.2.23-001.comment: Both the vehicle owner and the driver are responsible for the roadworthy condition of a vehicle. The driver must check the operational and traffic safety of the vehicle before driving. The owner must ensure this happens, including the TÜV inspection. The liability insurance is not responsible.

1.2.23-002.question_text: What should you do if you find out your vehicle is no longer roadworthy while driving?

options.text: Pull the vehicle off the road as quickly as possible
Only continue driving after fixing the issue
Drive to the next authorized workshop

1.2.23-002.comment: If a vehicle is not roadworthy, the driver must pull it off the road as quickly as possible. Keep in mind that driving to the next workshop is also prohibited. You can only continue driving after the issue has been fixed.

1.2.23-003.question_text: What vehicle defects can pose a danger to road traffic?

options.text: Worn tires
Broken tail lights
Insufficient braking power

1.2.23-003.comment: Worn tires reduce grip on the road and can cause the car to skid. Broken tail lights make the car less visible to other traffic. Insufficient braking power can lead to longer braking distances, increasing the risk of accidents, especially rear-end collisions. All three defects create a danger to traffic safety.

1.2.23-006.question_text: You want to make a phone call while driving. What should you consider?

options.text: The conversation can distract me
Using the phone can distract me
Using a hands-free device won't distract me

1.2.23-006.comment: Talking on the phone or using it can distract you from what's happening on the road. Even with a hands-free device, you should assume that part of your attention is diverted, and you can't fully focus on driving.

1.2.23-007.question_text: You want to make a phone call while driving. What do you need to keep in mind?

options.text: I need a hands-free device
I can call without a hands-free device if the car is parked safely and the engine is off
I can call without a hands-free device if the car is moving slowly

1.2.23-007.comment: You can only make calls using a hands-free device while driving. If you don't have one, you must pull over safely and turn off the engine before using your phone. Calling while driving without a hands-free device is a serious violation, classified as an A-offense, with heavy penalties.

1.2.23-008.question_text: You want to operate a motor vehicle on public roads. What must you consider?

options.text: The vehicle must be roadworthy
There must be liability insurance for the vehicle
I must be the vehicle owner

1.2.23-008.comment: You can only operate a motor vehicle on public roads if it is roadworthy and has liability insurance.

1.2.26-005.question_text: What applies immediately before and on pedestrian crossings?

options.text: - overtaking is prohibited
- stopping is required
- parking is allowed

1.2.26-005.comment: There's a strict no-overtaking rule before and on pedestrian crossings. This is to ensure that drivers have a clear view of the crossing and any pedestrians. Parking and stopping within five meters before and on the crossing is not allowed. Always approach pedestrian crossings with caution.

options.text: I stop because a man wants to cross the pedestrian crossing
I continue slowly because no pedestrian is visible
I stop because a child will step onto the road behind the van

1.2.26-007.comment: At a pedestrian crossing, you must allow pedestrians to cross the road. A pedestrian coming from the right may run onto the street quickly. Approach at a moderate speed and be ready to stop if necessary.

options.text: - do not overtake
- overtake, as there's no oncoming traffic
- only overtake at a moderate speed

1.2.26-008-M.comment: You are at a pedestrian crossing. In this situation, you must not overtake cyclists before or at the crossing.

1.2.26-009-M.question_text: What should you expect with such crossing aids?

options.text: Pedestrians assume they have priority over traffic
Cyclists cross the street without paying attention to traffic
Pedestrians always respect the priority of vehicles

1.2.26-009-M.comment: Cyclists and pedestrians often think they have the right of way. So, be especially attentive.

1.2.26-010-M.question_text: How should you behave correctly in this situation?

options.text: I watch the pedestrians closely
I reduce my speed and prepare to stop
I continue at the same speed

1.2.26-010-M.comment: Pedestrians always have the right of way at crossings, so you need to watch them closely and be ready to slow down and stop.

1.2.26-108.question_text: The traffic light is green. You want to turn right. How do you behave towards people crossing the street you want to turn into?

options.text: Allow people to cross the street
Turn quickly in front of the people
Honk to warn the people

1.2.26-108.comment: If a driver wants to turn right and the light is green, they must stop if pedestrians are crossing, regardless of how many there are. If the cross traffic is red, pedestrian signals on the side street usually show green. Even without a signal, pedestrians have the right of way, and drivers must stop and wait. Cyclists riding straight next to the driver or coming towards them also have priority and must be allowed to pass.

1.2.26-111.question_text: In which cases do you need to approach a pedestrian crossing with extra caution?

options.text: When pedestrians want to cross the road
When visibility of the pedestrian crossing is limited
When another vehicle is already waiting at the pedestrian crossing

1.2.26-111.comment: Drivers must approach a pedestrian crossing carefully. Extra caution is needed when people want to cross the road or when visibility is limited, for example, by a vehicle already waiting at the crossing. You must never overtake this vehicle.

1.2.26-113.question_text: A person wants to cross the road at the pedestrian crossing. How do you behave?

options.text: I prepare to stop
I don't overtake
I overtake waiting vehicles with special caution

1.2.26-113.comment: Approach the pedestrian crossing at a moderate speed and signal that you will wait. If you make eye contact with the pedestrian, reinforce this with gestures. If slowing down isn't enough to let the pedestrian cross, you must stop. You can't overtake any vehicle before or on pedestrian crossings.

1.2.26-114.question_text: How do you behave in this situation?

options.text: I let the pedestrian cross the road
I wait before the pedestrian crossing until the blue vehicle has turned
I close in on the blue vehicle immediately

1.2.26-114.comment: If a pedestrian clearly wants to cross the street at a pedestrian crossing, you need to approach at a moderate speed and wait. You can't stop on a pedestrian crossing in heavy traffic. In such cases, you also need to keep intersections and junctions clear.

1.2.26-115.question_text: Why is a defensive driving style especially important when approaching pedestrian crossings?

options.text: So pedestrians aren't confused
To avoid rear-end collisions
So following vehicles can overtake more easily

1.2.26-115.comment: Approaching defensively and slowing down shows pedestrians that you're ready to wait. This way, pedestrians can cross the road safely. Plus, by stopping in time, you can avoid rear-end collisions.

1.2.26-116.question_text: You're driving on a road with two lanes in one direction in the left lane. About 30 meters ahead, a truck is stopped in the right lane before a pedestrian crossing. How do you behave?

options.text: I approach at a moderate speed
I give warning signals and drive past the truck
I keep driving quickly

1.2.26-116.comment: You must never overtake a vehicle before or on pedestrian crossings. The truck blocks your view of the crossing. It might be letting pedestrians cross. Even if it's in another lane, you can't overtake it. Approach the pedestrian crossing at a moderate speed, ready to stop.

1.2.26-117.question_text: A cyclist wants to cross the road at a pedestrian crossing without getting off. How do you behave?

options.text: I let the cyclist pass
I honk and drive past the cyclist
I only brake shortly before the pedestrian crossing

1.2.26-117.comment: The cyclist is breaking the rules. They must get off before crossing the pedestrian crossing. However, as a driver approaching the crossing properly and cautiously, you shouldn't run them over. That would also be against the rules. You must stop for the cyclist at the pedestrian crossing if necessary and let them pass.

1.2.26-118.question_text: In front of you is a pedestrian crossing, behind which traffic is backed up in your lane. How do you behave?

options.text: Wait before the pedestrian crossing to let people cross
Wait on the pedestrian crossing if no people are visible
Wait on the pedestrian crossing to reduce the vehicle backlog

1.2.26-118.comment: In heavy traffic, you must not stop on a pedestrian crossing. The same rule applies as at intersections and junctions, which must also be kept clear.

options.text: I wait because both pedestrians have the right of way
I keep driving because both pedestrians have to wait
I turn before the oncoming pedestrian because only they have to wait

1.2.26-119-M.comment: If you encounter pedestrians wanting to cross the street while turning, you need to be considerate. You must stop and wait before turning.

options.text: - leave the ignition key or transponder in the vehicle
- exit the tunnel through the emergency exit
- wait in the vehicle for the accident site to be cleared

1.2.34-004.comment: If there's an accident in the tunnel and at least one car is on fire with smoke, you need to stop and leave your car. You can exit the tunnel through the emergency exit and follow the emergency lights. If there are none, you should feel your way along the tunnel wall. Since the fire department might need to move your car, you should leave the ignition key or transponder in the vehicle.

1.2.34-006.question_text: You're involved in an accident. What document must you show to other parties if they ask for it?

options.text: Your driver's license
The vehicle registration certificate Part I or the operating permit
The liability insurance contract

1.2.34-006.comment: In a traffic accident, all parties must show the following documents if asked: driver's license and the vehicle registration certificate Part I (Fahrzeugschein) or the operating permit. You also need to provide information about your liability insurance to the best of your knowledge.

1.2.34-007.question_text: You're the first to arrive at an accident scene with injuries. You've secured the scene and assessed the situation. What else do you need to do?

options.text: - provide first aid to the injured
- alert emergency services
- document the accident

1.2.34-007.comment: Before you attend to the injured, you need to alert emergency services. After that, you're required to provide first aid to the injured.

1.2.34-008.question_text: You're involved in an accident in a parking lot with minor damage. All parties decide not to inform the police. What is helpful for settling the damage now?

options.text: Taking photos of the accident scene from multiple angles
Exchanging necessary information among the parties
Describing the accident in the accident report

1.2.34-008.comment: You should exchange important information with the other party to stay in contact. You should also agree on documenting the accident details. Taking photos of the damage helps the insurance assess and evaluate the situation better.

1.2.34-009.question_text: You've damaged someone else's parked vehicle with your car. After waiting a reasonable time, the owner hasn't shown up. What should you do now?

options.text: - leave your name and address at the accident site
- report the accident to the police
- tell an uninvolved witness your name and address

1.2.34-009.comment: According to StVO § 34 6. a) - 7., after a reasonable waiting time, you can leave the accident scene if you've left your name and address at the site and reported the accident to the police.

1.2.34-103.question_text: You're the first to arrive at an accident scene with injuries. What should you generally do first?

options.text: Secure the accident scene
Drive to the nearest phone booth and alert emergency services
Check how serious the injuries are

1.2.34-103.comment: If you're the first to reach an accident scene with injuries, stay calm and secure the accident scene first. This helps prevent further accidents and protects the injured. Then check on the injured and provide first aid. Inform emergency services.

1.2.34-106.question_text: How can you request help on the highway?

options.text: At highway rest areas
At emergency call stations
By calling 112 or 110

1.2.34-106.comment: In case of a breakdown or accident on the highway, you can request help at the emergency call station or by calling 112 or 110. If your vehicle can make it to the next rest area, you can also call for help there.

1.2.34-109.question_text: You notice an accident in the tunnel. What should you do?

options.text: Turn on your hazard lights
Inform emergency services via the emergency call station
Do not leave your vehicle

1.2.34-109.comment: In case of an accident in the tunnel, drivers are required to immediately activate their hazard lights to warn following traffic. Park your vehicle on the right side of the road or, if possible, in a lay-by, and carefully exit to inspect the accident scene and make an emergency call. Secure the accident scene and provide first aid. Also, pay attention to your own safety, emergency exits, and emergency call phones.

1.2.34-110.question_text: You're involved in a traffic accident. What are you required to do?

options.text: - immediately move to the side if damage is minor
- inform the other parties that you were also involved in the accident
- provide your name and address to the entitled parties upon request

1.2.34-110.comment: If the damage is minor, the person responsible for the accident must move to the side immediately to avoid causing traffic jams and further dangers. They also have to inform the other parties that they were involved in the accident. Failing to do so is considered a hit-and-run and is punishable by law, which can lead to a criminal record and loss of your driver's license. They must also provide their name and address to those entitled. These are just some of the obligations of an accident-causing driver.

1.2.34-111.question_text: You've had an accident on a country road. How do you secure the accident scene?

options.text: I turn on the hazard lights immediately
I place the warning triangle visibly about 100 meters before the accident site
I warn other vehicles if necessary, for example, with hand signals

1.2.34-111.comment: Turning on the hazard lights is the first step, but it's not enough to secure the accident scene. The warning triangle should be set up about 100 meters before the accident site outside of towns. If needed, warn other road users with hand signals, as long as it doesn't put anyone, including yourself, in danger.

1.2.34-112.question_text: How can you find the shortest way to the nearest emergency call box on highways?

options.text: - black arrows on the guide posts
- directional markings on the guardrails
- ground markings on the hard shoulder

1.2.34-112.comment: You can find the shortest way to the nearest emergency call box by looking for the black arrows (directional triangles) on the guide posts. They indicate the way on highways.

1.2.34-113.question_text: What are you required to do if you're involved in a traffic accident?

options.text: - stop and check the consequences of the accident
- secure the accident scene
- provide help if there are injuries

1.2.34-113.comment: After an accident, drivers and all other involved parties must stop and check the consequences. Make sure to secure the accident scene immediately or help with that to avoid further damage. Then provide first aid to the injured.

1.2.34-114.question_text: A driver has slightly damaged another vehicle and leaves the scene without permission. What can be the consequence?

options.text: A fine or prison sentence
A withdrawal of the driving license or a driving ban
An order for a medical-psychological examination

1.2.34-114.comment: If you leave the scene of an accident, you're committing a hit-and-run. According to the criminal code, this can lead to a fine or a prison sentence of up to three years. After a hit-and-run, you might also get points on your record, a driving ban of up to three months, or lose your driving license. A medical-psychological examination can also be ordered for serious violations.

1.2.36-001.question_text: A police officer is directing traffic at an intersection, even though the traffic lights are working. What applies?

options.text: The signals from the police officer
The traffic light signals
The right of way traffic signs

1.2.36-001.comment: In traffic regulation, there's a set hierarchy you need to follow. A police officer's signals take precedence over everything else. Then you follow the traffic light signals, which are above the traffic signs. If there are no signs, lights, or police, the rule 'right before left' applies.

1.2.36-003.question_text: What do instructions from police officers mean?

options.text: You must follow them
You only have to follow them if they match the traffic signs
They relieve you of your duty of care

1.2.36-003.comment: Drivers must always follow the signals and instructions from police officers. Other rules and signals like traffic lights or signs take a back seat. However, drivers shouldn't neglect their duty of care.

options.text: The yellow car must clear the intersection
I must prepare to continue driving
I can turn now

1.2.36-004-B.comment: The police officer gives traffic instructions through their body position and specific arm movements. An arm raised means that drivers at the intersection cannot continue, and those previously blocked should prepare to move. The officer spreads their arms away from the body or keeps them close, depending on the instruction. If the officer faces the driver, they must stop. If the officer is sideways and the driver sees their profile, the driver can continue at a moderate speed.

1.2.36-007.question_text: In your rearview mirror, you see a police car directly behind you with red letters saying 'STOP POLICE'. Who does this apply to?

options.text: Only you
For all following vehicles
For all vehicles on the road

1.2.36-007.comment: Since the instruction is directed forward and you are the next vehicle in front of the police car, it applies to you. You're legally required to follow these instructions from the police.

1.2.36-011.question_text: A police car passes you and cuts in right in front of you. A sign on the roof says in red lights 'PLEASE FOLLOW'. What should you do?

options.text: - follow the police car
- stop if the police car stops
- keep the engine running after stopping

1.2.36-011.comment: The 'PLEASE FOLLOW' signal is meant for the driver directly behind the police car. So, you need to follow the police's instructions, drive behind them, and stop when they do.

1.2.36-012.question_text: A police car passes you and cuts in right in front of you. A sign on the roof says in red lights 'PLEASE FOLLOW'. Who does this apply to?

options.text: For me
For all vehicles in my lane
For following police and emergency vehicles

1.2.36-012.comment: The 'PLEASE FOLLOW' signal on a police car applies to the vehicle directly behind it, which is you in this case. The police can stop you for a traffic check. Follow the police car and stop when it stops.

1.2.36-013.question_text: A vehicle directly in front of you signals you with a 'police baton'. What does this mean?

options.text: I must follow the vehicle until it stops
I can't overtake the vehicle
I must turn in the indicated direction

1.2.36-013.comment: Generally, the driver behind the police vehicle must follow the signal given by the police. If it's clear, the police baton can also apply to drivers ahead. You can't overtake the police car and must follow it.

options.text: I cross the intersection carefully
I wait at the intersection for further instructions from the officer
I let the blue vehicle go first

1.2.36-014-M.comment: The police officer has the highest authority in traffic rules here. The basic rule of 'right before left', traffic signs, and traffic lights don't apply at this moment. Still, stay alert because other road users might behave incorrectly.

options.text: The red car
The motorcycle
Me

1.2.36-015-M.comment: Traffic is being controlled by the police, so the red car gets to go first.

options.text: The intersection can be crossed
I must wait for further signals from the officer before entering the intersection
Turning is not allowed

1.2.36-101-B.comment: The gestures of the traffic officer dictate how to behave. If the officer is standing sideways to your direction and you see their profile, you can continue and turn right. Right turners should cross the intersection quickly unless a pedestrian or cyclist is coming. If you want to turn left, enter the intersection to ensure a smooth traffic flow and wait for the officer's instructions.

options.text: The green car must wait
I can turn after observing the traffic signs
I can only turn when the light is green

1.2.37-002-B.comment: The traffic light controls the right of way for straight-moving traffic. The left turn lane doesn't have its own light. When turning left, you need to enter the intersection and wait for a gap in oncoming traffic to proceed. For the right turn lane that branches off earlier, the traffic sign takes precedence over the light. Watch out for cross traffic when turning.

1.2.37-009.question_text: Where must you stop before turning right at this traffic light with a green arrow sign?

options.text: At the stop line
If there's no stop line, before the intersection or junction
You don't have to stop

1.2.37-009.comment: You must stop at the stop line. If there isn't one, you must stop before the intersection or junction. If traffic conditions allow, you can turn right even when the light is red. When turning right at a red light, you should act as if at a 'stop yield' sign. You must yield to cross traffic.

1.2.37-010-M.question_text: How do you behave in this situation?

options.text: Cross the intersection without stopping
Stop at the sight line
Stop at the stop line

1.2.37-010-M.comment: The traffic light takes precedence over other traffic signs and road markings. Cross the intersection quickly without stopping since the light is green.

1.2.37-011-M.question_text: Where do you need to wait?

options.text: At the stop line
At the visibility line
At the traffic light

1.2.37-011-M.comment: When a traffic light is on, it takes priority over signs that regulate right of way. If there's a stop line, you need to stop there and wait until you can go.

options.text: Right turners may go
Straight drivers may go
Left turners may go

1.2.37-012-M.comment: If the light is red, drivers wanting to go straight or turn left must stop and wait. If there's an additional light with a green arrow pointing right, right turners are allowed to proceed. A light without extra signals applies to all directions.

options.text: Keep going
Slow down

1.2.37-013.comment: The light just changed from green to yellow right in front of you. You're going 45 km/h, which is too fast to stop before the light. Plus, there's a truck behind you that could rear-end you if you brake suddenly. So, keep going.

options.text: I can turn without hindrance
I must let oncoming traffic go
I must stop in the middle of the intersection

1.2.37-015.comment: As a driver turning left, you generally have to give way to oncoming traffic. Since there's a green clearance arrow on the opposite corner, you can assume the light is red for oncoming traffic. So, you can turn.

options.text: Slow down
Keep going

1.2.37-017.comment: You see a traffic light changing from green to yellow ahead. You're approaching it at 40 km/h. Since you're still far enough from the light, you need to slow down.

options.text: I give way to possible cross traffic
I wait at the stop line for the next green phase
I quickly cross the intersection since 'yellow' is showing

1.2.37-018.comment: When the yellow light is flashing, the traffic light is out of service. The general right of way rules apply. Since you're not on the main road, possible cross traffic has the right of way.

1.2.37-019.question_text: Under what circumstances can you run a red light at an intersection?

options.text: To carefully make way for an emergency vehicle with flashing blue lights and sirens
