2.1.02-002.comment: To answer this question, you first need to calculate the reaction distance and the emergency braking distance. At 50 km/h, the reaction distance is 50 / 10 x 3 = 15 meters. So, the reaction distance is 15 meters. The emergency braking distance is calculated as follows: (50 / 10 x 50 / 10) / 2 = 12.5. So, 50 km/h is the correct answer.

2.1.02-003.question_text: Why do you need to brake?

options.text: Because a person is running onto the road
Because passengers are getting off the tram
Because the truck is changing into my lane

2.1.02-003.comment: In the video, you can see a person (coming from the right) running onto the road. Pay attention to this and brake in time.

2.1.02-005-M.question_text: What should you expect in this situation?

options.text: Children running onto the road
People getting off on the roadside
There’s a pedestrian crossing ahead

2.1.02-005-M.comment: The traffic sign indicates that you should be extra cautious of children who might run onto the road between vehicles. You also need to expect that people might get off on the roadside.

2.1.03-015.question_text: What can lead to aquaplaning (water slick) on a wet road?

options.text: High speed
Worn tires
Ruts in the road

2.1.03-015.comment: Aquaplaning, also known as water slick, happens when the tread depth of the tires is too low to displace the accumulated water, or when the amount of water to be displaced is too large due to high speed (from 60 km/h). Additionally, ruts in the road where water collects can further contribute to this effect.

2.1.03-025.question_text: What can a sudden deterioration of the road condition lead to?

options.text: To skidding and slipping hazards
To changed tire noises
To longer reaction times

2.1.03-025.comment: When the road surface deteriorates, it always results in a change and worsening of grip. As the tires lose traction, the vehicle can skid and slip more easily. Tire noises also depend on the condition of the road surface and change when the road, for example, goes from asphalt to cobblestones.

options.text: I brake
I drive as far right as possible
I stay in the middle of my lane

2.1.03-028.comment: While overtaking a cyclist, an oncoming truck might partially enter your lane. So, slow down and drive as far right as you can.

options.text: - green car
- blue car
- tractor

2.1.03-029.comment: You can barely see a green car coming from the right. So, please brake in time because, in these road conditions, your braking distance can increase significantly.

2.1.03-033.question_text: How should you behave correctly now?

options.text: I reduce my speed
I avoid sudden steering movements
I steer sharply to the right

2.1.03-033.comment: Due to the bad weather conditions, you should reduce your speed and avoid sudden steering movements (as indicated by the warning sign), otherwise, you could skid.

options.text: Limited steering ability of the vehicle
Reduced braking ability of the vehicle
Increased tire grip

2.1.03-034.comment: During aquaplaning, your vehicle loses direct contact with the road surface, so you can't steer or brake effectively.

2.1.03-036.question_text: How should you behave correctly in this situation?

options.text: I reduce my speed
I avoid sudden steering
I brake hard

2.1.03-036.comment: The traffic sign indicates a risk of skidding and slipping. To avoid skidding, you should reduce your speed, especially when it's raining and leaves are falling on the road. Hard braking, rapid acceleration, or sudden steering can cause your tires to lose grip, leading to skidding.

2.1.03-037.question_text: What should you prepare for here?

options.text: A longer braking distance
Poor visibility of my vehicle
Increased tire grip

2.1.03-037.comment: Because of the rain, you should expect that other road users might not see your vehicle well, and your braking distance will increase due to reduced tire grip.

2.1.03-038.question_text: When are you particularly at risk during the overtaking maneuver here?

options.text: When entering the truck's slipstream
When exiting the truck's slipstream
When changing lanes after overtaking

2.1.03-038.comment: If there's strong crosswind from the right, you're particularly at risk when you move from open road into the slipstream of a truck during an overtaking maneuver. The strong wind pushes your vehicle to the left, causing you to steer against it. While overtaking, you enter the truck's slipstream, and the crosswind disappears, so you need to adjust your steering. Once you exit the slipstream, the crosswind pressure returns, and you have to steer against it again.

2.1.03-101.question_text: Where does aquaplaning occur most frequently?

options.text: In road depressions
At ruts in the road
At level crossings

2.1.03-101.comment: Aquaplaning happens when your speed is too high and/or there's more water than your tire treads can handle. A layer of water prevents tire contact with the road, making the vehicle uncontrollable. The risk of aquaplaning is particularly high in ruts and road depressions. At level crossings, there's usually no increased risk of aquaplaning since water can drain well there.

2.1.03-103.question_text: What should you expect when it starts to rain after a long dry spell?

options.text: A dangerous slippery layer on the road
Worse visibility right after turning on the wipers
A shorter braking distance

2.1.03-103.comment: When it starts to rain after a long dry period, a slippery film forms on the road that only washes away after a while. This film is more dangerous than rain alone. Brake very carefully. This slippery film also builds up on your windshield, making visibility worse right after you turn on the wipers. The braking distance increases because of the reduced grip.

2.1.03-104.question_text: It starts to rain. Why do you need to increase your following distance immediately?

options.text: Because a slippery film can form, increasing the braking distance
Because visibility can get worse and the wipers won't clear the view right away
Because the brakes respond faster

2.1.03-104.comment: When it starts to rain, you need to increase your following distance for several reasons: Wet conditions turn dirt, dust, and fine debris on the road into a dangerous slippery film. This reduces grip and increases braking distance. This slippery film also forms on your windshield and brake drums. When you activate the wipers, they can smear the glass and impair your visibility. On brake drums, this film can slow down brake response in wet conditions.

2.1.03-105.question_text: You're driving on a federal road outside of town in thick fog. Are you allowed to drive over the center line constantly?

options.text: No, because it can endanger oncoming traffic
Yes, if fog lights and rear fog lights are on
Yes, because it reduces the risk of going off the road

2.1.03-105.comment: Driving on the center line is not allowed even in thick fog, especially since drivers may collide with oncoming traffic due to reduced visibility. Slow down in fog and stay close to the right edge of the road for a safe drive.

2.1.03-106.question_text: What should you do during the day when a fog bank suddenly appears?

options.text: Immediately adjust your speed to the visibility conditions
Turn on your low beam headlights
Only turn on your parking lights

2.1.03-106.comment: As a driver, you must turn on your low beam headlights during the day in fog, snowfall, and other poor visibility conditions. Driving with just parking lights is not allowed because they don't provide enough light. Adjust your speed to the visibility and use your fog lights if visibility is under 50 meters.

2.1.03-107.question_text: How can you ensure good visibility through the windshield?

options.text: In fog, turn on the wipers from time to time
In slushy snow, turn on the wipers before other vehicles throw slush on your windshield
When the inside of the windshield fogs up, turn off the ventilation and keep the windows closed

2.1.03-107.comment: In fog, set your wipers to intermittent to remove fine water droplets. Before overtaking or being overtaken, adjust your wipers to clear any slush or spray immediately. To avoid fogging inside the windshield, set the ventilation to bring in outside air instead of recirculating. Crack the windows slightly to let moisture escape. Briefly turning on the air conditioning can quickly dehumidify the air.

2.1.03-111.question_text: You've found yourself in this situation while overtaking several trucks. How do you behave now?

options.text: I cancel the overtaking maneuver
I ensure a safe following distance after merging back in
I continue to overtake quickly and merge in front of the red truck

2.1.03-111.comment: Visibility is very poor due to the weather, and the road isn't clearly visible. To avoid endangering anyone, you should cancel the overtaking maneuver as quickly as possible and ensure a safe distance when merging back in.

options.text: I continue to slow down
I wait before the obstacle
I switch to the left now

2.1.03-115.comment: Since a vehicle is coming from behind in the left lane, please wait before the obstacle (snow drift ahead) and continue to slow down.

options.text: - reduce speed significantly
- continue driving in my lane
- drive left past the road damage

2.1.03-116-M.comment: Here, you should significantly reduce your speed due to poor visibility and continue driving in your lane. Passing on the left is not a good idea, as someone might be coming from the opposite direction.

2.1.03-117.question_text: You're driving on the highway. What is correct in this situation?

options.text: - turn on the rear fog light
- drive no faster than 50 km/h
- drive no faster than 80 km/h

2.1.03-117.comment: With severely limited visibility on the highway, you can turn on your rear fog light and drive no faster than 50 km/h.

2.1.03-119.question_text: You're using your car's Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC) during this weather. What should you expect?

options.text: The ACC might not work properly
I need to control the speed and distance myself
The ACC will stop the vehicle

2.1.03-119.comment: The Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC) estimates the distance and speed of the car in front. In bad weather, like snow and dirt, its function can be limited. So, you need to manage the distance and speed yourself.

2.1.03-120.question_text: You're driving on a narrow avenue. What should you keep in mind?

options.text: I should be able to stop within half the visible distance
I might need to stop for oncoming traffic
I should expect uneven road edges from tree roots

2.1.03-120.comment: The narrow road and its often curved shape due to tree roots require extra caution in turns and with oncoming traffic. Choose your speed so you can stop within half the distance you can see. For example, if you can see about 40 meters ahead, you should be able to stop within about 20 meters. At 30 km/h, the stopping distance is around 18 meters.

2.1.03-121.question_text: The indicator for the Electronic Stability Control (ESC) has lit up several times. How should you react in this situation?

options.text: I reduce my speed, as it’s too high
I maintain my speed, as the ESC system allows for safe driving
I go to a workshop, as the ESC indicator suggests a defect

2.1.03-121.comment: You need to reduce your speed. The slippery road and your obviously too high speed for the current conditions can cause the wheels to lose grip, and your car could skid.

options.text: With pedestrians on the road
With reduced space from oncoming traffic
With glare from the low sun

2.1.03-122.comment: The snow on the sides of the road can narrow the driving lane. So, you should expect that the space between you and oncoming traffic is reduced. Also, the traffic sign indicates there's a parking area for hikers on the right, so you should expect pedestrians on the road.

2.1.03-123.question_text: While driving straight, you lose control of your vehicle due to aquaplaning. How should you react?

options.text: I gently lift my foot off the gas pedal
I keep the steering wheel as straight as possible
I brake hard

2.1.03-123.comment: During aquaplaning, you can't steer or change direction. You should neither accelerate nor brake. So, just gently lift your foot off the gas and try to keep the steering wheel straight until your tires regain contact with the road.

2.1.04-002.question_text: What should you do if wild animals suddenly appear in your high beams?

options.text: Switch to low beams immediately
Honk and brake
Keep driving with high beams unchanged

2.1.04-002.comment: Hold the steering wheel firmly and brake. Switch off the high beams, as they can blind the animals and cause them to stay on the road. Honk to scare them away. Avoid swerving at high speeds, as that can lead to hitting a tree or oncoming traffic. So, when you see wild animals on the road: brake, switch to low beams, and then honk to scare them away.

2.1.04-102.question_text: At night and in the rain, vehicles with low beams are coming towards you on a country road. What should you consider?

options.text: You might be blinded by reflections on the wet road
Visibility worsens due to streaks on the windshield
You can avoid glare by turning on high beams

2.1.04-102.comment: You shouldn't turn on your high beams in this situation, as that can blind oncoming traffic. Especially on wet roads, light reflections are significantly increased. Other issues include water droplets and streaks on the windshield that scatter the light and impair visibility.

2.1.04-103.question_text: What dangers can arise if you drive with your high beams on?

options.text: Oncoming drivers will be blinded
Wild animals on the road will be blinded and stay in the light
Abandoned vehicles on my side of the road will be recognized too late

2.1.04-103.comment: With your high beams on, you can blind drivers ahead and coming towards you, which might cause them to miss pedestrians and cyclists. Wild animals crossing the road can also be blinded, causing them to freeze in the light. You yourself will notice abandoned vehicles more easily with high beams.

2.1.04-104.question_text: At night on a country road, you see people on your side of the road. How should you behave if you're blinded by an oncoming vehicle?

options.text: - look towards the right edge of the road
- stop if necessary
- turn on high beams

2.1.04-104.comment: If you see people on the road at night, reduce your speed. Regularly looking at the road edge is ideal to avoid an accident. If you're also blinded, you can pull over to the right and stop.

2.1.05-002.question_text: What can long driving at higher speeds lead to?

options.text: You lose your sense of speed
You tailgate too closely
Your reaction readiness increases

2.1.05-002.comment: When you drive fast for a long time, your senses get used to it, and you start underestimating your speed. This is why people often take sharp turns off the highway too quickly. Fast, monotonous driving can reduce your concentration and reaction time. Often, drivers ignore the safe distance and tailgate.

2.1.05-008.question_text: You're approaching a tight left turn at high speed. Why do you need to slow down before the turn?

options.text: You could slide out of the curve to the right
You could skid
You could slide out of the curve to the left

2.1.05-008.comment: At high speed, centrifugal force can cause your vehicle to slide out of the curve to the right and skid. That's why you should slow down before the turn.

2.1.05-009.question_text: In what situation is your own speed often underestimated?

options.text: On wide and well-built roads
After a long drive at higher speeds
On narrow roads with uneven surfaces

2.1.05-009.comment: When you drive steadily at high speeds, your concentration decreases. You get used to the speed. Wide roads with little surrounding development can also make you less aware of how fast you're actually going. Your reaction time gets longer.

2.1.05-101.question_text: What is particularly important when choosing your speed on narrow avenues?

options.text: Estimating the side distance to trees and oncoming traffic
That you might have to stop in the visible distance for oncoming wide vehicles
Quickly changing light conditions make estimating side distances easier

2.1.05-101.comment: When driving on narrow avenues, you need to consider factors like changing light conditions due to the trees. This makes it harder to judge the distances to the sides and oncoming traffic. You should choose a speed that allows you to stop within the distance you can see ahead. This is especially important since wide or tall vehicles often drive in the middle of the road.

2.1.05-105-M.question_text: What should you expect in this situation?

options.text: A slow-moving vehicle in my lane
Oncoming traffic cutting the corner
Wild animals crossing

2.1.05-105-M.comment: Since visibility is severely limited, be on the lookout for oncoming traffic cutting the corner, a slow-moving vehicle in your lane, and wild animals crossing.

2.1.06-007-M.question_text: You want to overtake. What should you do now?

options.text: I give up on overtaking
I speed up
I maintain my speed

2.1.06-007-M.comment: Since the vehicle behind you has already started to overtake, you should give up on overtaking.

2.1.06-008-M.question_text: You want to overtake. What should you pay attention to?

options.text: only if I can see the required distance
only if no vehicle is coming towards me
at the same time as the blue car

2.1.06-008-M.comment: You can overtake if you can see the required distance and if no vehicle is coming towards you (limited visibility).

2.1.06-011.question_text: Why do you need to brake hard now?

options.text: Because of the car
Because of the truck
Because of the tractor

2.1.06-011.comment: Since the blue car is likely to come into your lane, you need to brake hard immediately and stay as far to the right as possible.

options.text: I overtake the blue car and then switch to the middle lane
I overtake the red van and then switch to the middle lane
I signal the following driver to keep more distance by lightly braking

2.1.06-012-M.comment: As the driver, you don't need to move to the middle lane just because another car is pressuring you from behind or using their high beams. You should overtake the blue car and the red van as usual. To safely switch to the middle lane, you need to complete the overtaking first.

2.1.06-013.question_text: You want to overtake. How should you behave correctly now?

options.text: I cancel the overtaking and stay behind the truck
I speed up and continue overtaking quickly
I maintain my speed and continue overtaking

2.1.06-013.comment: You've already signaled and want to overtake the truck. In your rearview mirror, you see a red car approaching quickly in the left lane. You need to immediately cancel the overtaking and stay behind the truck. If you continue, you could force the red car to brake hard, which might lead to a collision.

options.text: I continue the overtaking quickly
I cancel the overtaking and pull back to the right
I brake but continue the overtaking

2.1.06-014.comment: When vehicles are approaching quickly from behind, stay calm, finish the overtaking, and clear the lane at the next opportunity.

options.text: I overtake the van and then switch to the middle lane
I immediately switch to the right lane
I signal the following driver to keep more distance by lightly braking

2.1.06-015.comment: A driver in a car is tailgating you dangerously in the left lane and is signaling their intention to overtake with their high beams. You should overtake the van in the middle lane and then position yourself in front of it to ease the situation.

2.1.06-017-M.question_text: Why do you need to slow down here?

options.text: Because of the overtaking car
Because the speed limit is 80 km/h
Because of the tractor

2.1.06-017-M.comment: The oncoming car is overtaking despite the oncoming traffic about 250 meters ahead of you. You need to reduce your speed and move to the far right. This way, you ease the situation and give the overtaking car more time and space to finish overtaking and merge back in. The tractor is moving away from the intersection and poses no danger.

options.text: I slow down
I drive as far right as possible
I speed up

2.1.06-018-M.comment: If you're overtaking a vehicle while there's oncoming traffic, you should slow down and try to stay as far right as possible. This gives the other vehicle enough space to complete the overtaking safely.

2.1.06-021-M.question_text: You want to overtake. How should you behave correctly now?

options.text: I don't overtake the truck because I can't see the necessary distance
I follow the motorcycle since the truck is signaling an overtaking opportunity
I reduce the distance to the truck so I can overtake faster

2.1.06-021-M.comment: You shouldn't overtake the truck because you can't see the necessary distance.

2.1.06-023-M.question_text: How should you behave correctly now?

options.text: - not, because the tractor will pull left
- carefully, since the tractor is signaling me to do so
- immediately, since the overtaking path is sufficient

2.1.06-023-M.comment: You shouldn't overtake because the tractor will pull left (see blinker).

2.1.06-024-M.question_text: You want to overtake. How should you behave correctly here?

options.text: I don't overtake because the yellow vehicle could be overtaking
I don't overtake because oncoming traffic could appear
I overtake because there's no oncoming traffic visible

2.1.06-024-M.comment: The right behavior (looking ahead) here is not to overtake because the yellow vehicle could be overtaking and oncoming traffic could appear (limited visibility).

2.1.06-026-M.question_text: Why are you not allowed to overtake now?

options.text: - motorcycle
- road layout
- red cars

2.1.06-026-M.comment: You can't overtake the cyclist because of the motorcycle (oncoming traffic) and the road layout, which results in poor visibility.

2.1.06-027-M.question_text: Why are you not allowed to overtake now?

options.text: - motorcycle
- red cars
- posted no-overtaking sign

2.1.06-027-M.comment: At this moment, a motorcyclist is passing the tractor. Wait until you can start the overtaking maneuver safely.

2.1.06-028-M.question_text: Why are you not allowed to overtake here?

options.text: - I can't see the further road layout well enough
- I can't maintain enough side distance from the cyclists with oncoming traffic
- I can't cross the guideline

2.1.06-028-M.comment: Because of the curve and the trees, you can't see the further road layout well enough. Outside built-up areas, you must maintain a minimum side distance of 2 meters from cyclists. If oncoming traffic suddenly appears, you might not be able to maintain that distance while overtaking. That's why you can't overtake here.

2.1.06-029-M.question_text: Why are you not allowed to overtake here?

options.text: Because the side distance to the cyclists becomes too small
Because there's a risk to oncoming traffic
Because the guideline can't be crossed

2.1.06-029-M.comment: The road is too narrow to maintain enough side distance to both the cyclists and oncoming traffic.

2.1.06-030.question_text: You're about to overtake on a tree-lined avenue. What special thing should you keep in mind?

options.text: Side distances are often misjudged here
Vehicles with high bodies often avoid branches
The frequency of tree accidents is particularly high here

2.1.06-030.comment: The avenue is lined with trees, which can make it easy to misjudge distances because of the changing light and shadows. There can also be accidents with trees and vehicles with high bodies trying to avoid branches.

2.1.06-103-M.question_text: Why do you need to switch to the right lane now?

options.text: - red cars
- blue cars
- yellow tractor

2.1.06-103-M.comment: The traffic sign shows a narrowing (end of a lane) in 200 meters. The lane will lead into oncoming traffic due to the narrowing, so you need to be especially alert to avoid ending up in the wrong lane.

options.text: I won't overtake the cyclists for now
I will overtake the cyclists
I will honk to get the cyclists to ride single file

2.1.06-104-M.comment: You shouldn't overtake for now because they're riding side by side, and you can't maintain enough distance.

2.1.06-105.question_text: How should you behave correctly now?

options.text: I slow down to walking speed
I drive as far right as possible
I drive past the pedestrians

2.1.06-105.comment: In this situation, you need to slow down to walking speed and keep as far right as possible. You shouldn't drive past the pedestrians because it poses too much danger.

2.1.06-106-M.question_text: How should you behave correctly now?

options.text: I reduce my speed
I keep my speed
I overtake the cyclist

2.1.06-106-M.comment: You need to reduce your speed because you can't maintain enough distance from the cyclist.

2.1.07-009-M.question_text: Why do you need to brake now?

options.text: - green vehicle
- motorcycle
- yellow car

2.1.07-009-M.comment: You should brake because the green vehicle seems to be coming onto the road behind the tractor.

2.1.07-010-M.question_text: What should you expect in this parking lot?

options.text: With incorrectly parked trucks
With vehicles pulling out
With people on the road

2.1.07-010-M.comment: Vehicles can leave the parking lot, so watch out for vehicles pulling out. People might walk on the road because they're taking a break. Truck drivers often park in car parking spaces.

2.1.07-014-M.question_text: What should you expect in this situation?

options.text: The driver of the red vehicle might not see me
The green truck is turning around
The tractor is driving on the road

2.1.07-014-M.comment: Because of the turning truck, the delivery van might not see you. Be ready to brake.

2.1.07-015-M.question_text: Why should you reduce your speed here?

options.text: Because the red car might swerve into my lane
Because more people might enter the road
Because the blue car might keep going

2.1.07-015-M.comment: It's unlikely that the car on the left lane will move since it seems to have broken down. Even if it does, it won't affect you. However, since there's a person on the road, you need to be especially careful. It's also possible that more people might get out of the vehicle and run onto the road. The parked car might be hidden by the bushes, or there might not be a warning triangle set up. The car behind you might not realize in time that the vehicle in front has stopped. So, you should drive cautiously and expect that the car behind might swerve into your lane.

options.text: I drive as far right as possible
I brake
I switch to the left lane

2.1.07-020.comment: The yellow car is coming towards you as a wrong-way driver on the highway. Drive as far right as you can and brake. To warn other road users, turn on your hazard lights.

2.1.07-022-M.question_text: How should you behave in this situation?

options.text: Keep reducing speed
Be ready to brake
Perform an emergency stop

2.1.07-022-M.comment: Animals on the road can be unpredictable. You should keep reducing your speed and pay close attention to the situation. If the animals run onto the road, you should be ready to brake. An emergency stop could lead to a rear-end collision if the vehicle behind you can't react quickly enough.

2.1.07-023-M.question_text: Why should you reduce your speed now?

options.text: Because of the animal
Because of the red car
Because of the speed limit

2.1.07-023-M.comment: Even if you're following the speed limit of 60 km/h, an animal is running onto the road right in front of you. To avoid an accident, you need to slow down. The oncoming car doesn't affect your driving.

2.1.07-101.question_text: When can a fast-moving car skid sideways on a dry, straight road?

options.text: When it's suddenly hit by strong crosswinds
When a tire bursts
When there's suddenly headwind

2.1.07-101.comment: A vehicle on a straight, dry road can skid sideways due to strong crosswinds or a burst tire. In that case, immediately ease off the gas, steer against it, and brake gently.

2.1.07-102.question_text: What makes driving in a convoy easier?

options.text: Watching the convoy through the windows of the vehicles ahead
Slightly offset driving in your own lane
Driving with hazard lights constantly on

2.1.07-102.comment: Slightly offset driving allows you to see the vehicles ahead. This way, you can see past the car in front or through its windows to assess the traffic situation and react more quickly to sudden events. Driving with hazard lights in a convoy is generally prohibited.

2.1.07-106.question_text: If a tire bursts while driving fast on the highway, how should you behave?

options.text: Ease off the gas, steer against it, and brake gently
Pull over to the shoulder, turn on hazard lights, and set up a warning triangle
Immediately perform a full brake and then switch to the shoulder

2.1.07-106.comment: Avoid a full brake on the highway; instead, steer against it and brake gently to stabilize your vehicle. If possible, bring your vehicle to a stop on the shoulder. Turn on your hazard lights and set up your warning triangle to warn following vehicles.

2.1.07-109.question_text: You increase your speed from 50 km/h to 100 km/h. How does the braking distance change according to the rule of thumb?

options.text: It quadruples from 25 m to 100 m
It doubles from 15 m to 30 m
It halves from 50 m to 25 m

2.1.07-109.comment: According to the rule of thumb, the braking distance quadruples when the speed doubles. For example, at 40 km/h, it's 16 meters, and at 80 km/h, it's 64 meters.

2.1.07-111.question_text: Why do you need to be ready to brake in this situation?

options.text: Because the other vehicle might keep going
Because the road layout requires it
Because a speed limit is visible

2.1.07-111.comment: You see a vehicle trying to enter the road from the right. Since it's coming from a field or forest path, you have the right of way. The trees might limit visibility for the driver. It's possible they might continue despite having to wait. That's why you need to be ready to brake until you clearly see that they stop.

2.1.07-112.question_text: Why should you reduce your speed now?

options.text: Because I'm hard to see for other road users
Because the road layout requires it
Because I need to yield the right of way

2.1.07-112.comment: You generally have the right of way since you're on a main road. However, to avoid a dangerous situation, you should still slow down and be ready to brake, as the driver of the car coming from the right might not see you in time or might completely overlook you. The trees at the roadside significantly limit their visibility.

2.1.07-113-M.question_text: How should you behave in this situation?

options.text: I slow down
I speed up
I keep driving at a steady speed

2.1.07-113-M.comment: Since the left lane is narrowing and the vehicle next to you is in that lane and needs to turn right, you should slow down here.

2.1.07-114-M.question_text: What should you expect in this situation?

options.text: - A motorcyclist braking
- A tractor continuing to drive
- A tractor waiting

2.1.07-114-M.comment: Even though you're on a main road, you should always be prepared for dangerous situations. The tractor driver approaching your road at an intersection might not yield and could force the vehicle in front of you to brake. By driving defensively, you can help avoid potentially dangerous situations.

2.1.07-115.question_text: How should you behave in this situation?

options.text: I maintain my speed and keep driving
I speed up to create a safe distance
I brake briefly so the driver behind can reduce speed

2.1.07-115.comment: In this situation, you should maintain your speed and keep driving as you are.

2.1.07-117-M.question_text: What do you need to pay attention to when turning right?

options.text: To the motorcycle
To vehicles coming from the left
To the tractor

2.1.07-117-M.comment: You must yield the right of way to all vehicles on the main road. The motorcycle is in the lane you want to turn into. Before you turn right onto the main road, you need to wait and let the motorcycle pass.

2.1.07-119.question_text: What should you do if a collision with wildlife is unavoidable?

options.text: I brake as hard as I can
I maintain my direction
I always swerve

2.1.07-119.comment: If a collision with an animal can't be avoided, you should maintain your direction. Brake hard and keep a firm grip on the steering wheel. Swerving can put other road users at risk or lead to greater damage than a controlled collision with the animal.

2.1.07-121-M.question_text: How should you behave in this situation?

options.text: I brake hard immediately
I don't swerve
I swerve to the left

2.1.07-121-M.comment: In this situation, you should brake hard immediately but also avoid swerving.

options.text: Reduce speed, be ready to brake
Switch to the left lane
Keep driving, signal your intention

2.1.07-202.comment: A car in front of you is parking. You need to reduce your speed and can only switch lanes to avoid the parking car after the motorcycle has passed you.

2.1.07-203.question_text: What do you need to know about using the rearview mirrors?

options.text: I can't see vehicles and pedestrians in the blind spot
Mirrors must be adjusted for the driver
The inside mirror has no blind spot to the right

2.1.07-203.comment: Here’s what you need to know about using rearview mirrors: 1. Before starting your drive, mirrors must be adjusted for the driver. 2. All types of mirrors have blind spots. These are areas you can't see where pedestrians, small vehicles, or obstacles can be missed. By properly adjusting the outside mirrors and the inside mirror, you can minimize the blind spot as much as possible.

2.1.07-206.question_text: You're on a country road. In front of you, there's a slow-moving line of about 15 vehicles. What should you do?

options.text: I'll stay behind the line of vehicles for now
I'll use my horn and blink to encourage those ahead to overtake
I'll overtake the line of vehicles as quickly as possible

2.1.07-206.comment: In such a convoy, it's important to stay calm and maintain a safe distance. Jumping from one vehicle to another, known as 'kolonnenspringen', won't save you time and increases the risk of accidents.

2.1.07-207.question_text: You're stopping your vehicle to let passengers out on the right. There's a bike path there. What should you do?

options.text: I should make sure no cyclists are coming
I should warn the passengers about the bike path
I should only watch the traffic in the rearview mirror

2.1.07-207.comment: As the driver, you have a special duty of care. So, if you're stopping with a passenger near a bike path, you should warn them about cyclists before they get out.

2.1.07-208.question_text: You're increasing your speed from 50 km/h to 100 km/h. How does the reaction distance change according to the rule of thumb?

options.text: It doubles from 15 m to 30 m
It quadruples from 25 m to 100 m
It halves from 50 m to 25 m

2.1.07-208.comment: When a driver doubles their speed, the reaction distance doubles from 15 to 30 meters.

options.text: A lane change by the vehicle ahead
Increased traffic behind the underpass
The end of the right lane

2.1.08-005-B.comment: The sign indicates the end of the left lane. The traffic flow will merge from two lanes to one. There may be stop-and-go traffic. The vehicle in the left lane will change lanes, so you need to let the vehicles from the ending left lane merge into your lane using the zipper principle.

2.1.08-008-B.question_text: A traffic jam is forming here. How should you behave correctly?

options.text: Turn on the hazard lights to warn following vehicles
Drive as far right as possible to create space for an emergency lane
Drive as far left as possible to create space for an emergency lane

2.1.08-008-B.comment: As you approach a traffic jam, turn on your hazard lights to alert other road users. It's important to create an emergency lane for any approaching emergency vehicles, so drive as far right as possible.

2.1.08-010.question_text: What should you expect when driving uphill on highways?

options.text: Slow-moving trucks in the right lane
Sudden overtaking maneuvers by other road users
Large speed differences between vehicles

2.1.08-010.comment: When driving uphill on highways, you should expect slow-moving trucks in the right lane, sudden overtaking maneuvers by other road users, and large speed differences between vehicles. All three answers are correct.

options.text: Slow down and stay in my lane
Switch to the left lane
Maintain speed and stay in my lane

2.1.08-011.comment: Since you're being overtaken by a car on the left, you need to stay in your lane and reduce your speed until the truck in front of you finishes its overtaking maneuver and moves back to the right lane.

2.1.08-013.question_text: What should you consider when entering the highway?

options.text: I can drive faster on the merging lane than on the main road
Traffic on the main road has the right of way
Traffic on the right main lane must allow me to merge

2.1.08-013.comment: On highways, the main traffic always has the right of way and doesn't have to allow merging. You can drive faster on the merging lane than the other vehicles.

2.1.08-014.question_text: You're driving at the recommended speed on the highway and want to exit at the next ramp. How should you behave?

options.text: I finish overtaking in good time
I significantly reduce my speed on the exit lane
I significantly reduce my speed already in the right lane of the highway

2.1.08-014.comment: Finish overtaking in good time and merge into the right lane. Before switching to the exit lane, check your surroundings and signal. On the exit lane, check your speed on the speedometer to judge it correctly. You should only reduce your speed significantly on the exit lane to avoid hindering traffic on the main road.

options.text: I slow down my vehicle
I turn on the hazard lights
I drive into the clear gap

2.1.08-016.comment: As you approach a traffic jam on the highway, you need to reduce your speed and warn drivers behind you by turning on your hazard lights. You should create a rescue lane.

2.1.08-018.question_text: What is correct in this situation?

options.text: I need to reduce my speed
The truck has the right of way
The truck has to wait

2.1.08-018.comment: The curve is hard to see for drivers. There could be other road users or obstacles on the road. So, it's wise to slow down before the curve and mentally prepare for a possible danger. This is also a tricky spot for oncoming drivers, so caution is necessary.

2.1.08-021.question_text: You're driving at least 20 km/h faster than the green truck. How should you behave?

options.text: I drive onto the highway in front of the green truck
I slow down and drive onto the highway behind the green truck
I stop at the end of the merging lane and drive onto the highway after the blue truck

2.1.08-021.comment: You're on a merging lane to the highway, previously called an acceleration lane. It's allowed to drive faster on the merging lane than the vehicles on the main lane. So, you can merge onto the highway in front of the green truck at a higher speed.

options.text: - not change lanes, as the red car is already changing
- into the middle lane, as my overtaking maneuver is complete
- change lanes, so I don't hinder the yellow car

2.1.08-024-M.comment: A red car is next to you, changing into the middle lane. Therefore, you can't change lanes, as it would endanger other road users.

2.1.08-025.question_text: You want to merge onto the highway. Which lane should you follow?
2.1.08-025.comment: You should choose line 3. Lines 1 and 2 are not correct.

2.1.08-026-M.question_text: What should you prepare for now?

options.text: The yellow car is leaving the highway
The motorcycle is leaving the highway
The blue bus in front of me is braking due to a traffic jam

2.1.08-026-M.comment: In this situation, there's no traffic jam in sight. Since the motorcycle is on the left, it won't be leaving the highway. However, the car on your left is signaling right. You should prepare for the driver to exit the highway.

2.1.08-027-M.question_text: You want to exit the highway. What creates a dangerous situation here?

options.text: The motorcycle
The yellow truck
The green vehicle

2.1.08-027-M.comment: The motorcycle behind you (as seen in the right mirror) creates a dangerous situation for you. Keep this in mind when leaving the highway.

options.text: I reduce my speed
I stay in the left lane
I continue driving as before

2.1.08-028-M.comment: There's an object on the road in front of the truck in the right lane. The truck will need to swerve to the left to avoid it. So, you should stay in the left lane. If you keep driving as you are, you might collide with the truck. That's why you should reduce your speed.

2.1.08-029-M.question_text: Why do you need to reduce your speed now?

options.text: Because of the truck
Because of the speed limit
Because of the blue car

2.1.08-029-M.comment: The right lane is blocked in front of the truck, and it needs to switch to the left lane. To let it do that, you should reduce your speed. The car behind you isn’t a reason to slow down. The speed limit here is 120 km/h, which you should stick to.

2.1.08-030-M.question_text: You want to leave the highway. How should you behave correctly?

options.text: I check my speed frequently using the speedometer
I reduce my speed from now on
I reduce my speed only when I reach the curve

2.1.08-030-M.comment: As soon as you enter the exit lane, you should start slowing down. If you slow down before entering the deceleration lane, you could disrupt traffic on the highway. You should check your speed often to make sure you're not going too fast into the curve. On highways, it's easy to get used to high speeds and then take an exit too quickly. If you only slow down at the curve, you might not reduce your speed in time. Generally, you should always slow down before a curve, not just in it.

2.1.08-031.question_text: Why should you stick to the recommended speed of 130 km/h on highways?

options.text: - To avoid accidents
- To reduce the severity of possible accidents
- To achieve a smooth traffic flow

2.1.08-031.comment: The higher the speed, the longer the reaction time and braking distance will be. When all vehicles travel at a similar speed, traffic flows more smoothly.

2.1.10-002.question_text: What helps combat fatigue on long trips?

options.text: Timely and sufficient breaks
Doing exercises during breaks
Drinking coffee instead of taking breaks

2.1.10-002.comment: Taking breaks in time helps prevent fatigue. Doing exercises during breaks gets your blood flowing and is good for your joints. Coffee only has a short-term stimulating effect, which can quickly turn into drowsiness, meaning you could fall asleep without warning.

2.1.10-004.question_text: What danger exists if you get distracted by using electronic devices while driving?

options.text: I can drift out of my lane
I can overlook traffic signs
My stopping distance can shorten

2.1.10-004.comment: Using electronic devices while driving can distract you, causing you to overlook traffic signs and drift out of your lane.

2.1.10-005.question_text: What causes so-called disco accidents among young drivers?

options.text: - Being overtired
- Being physically exhausted
- Being unfit to drive

2.1.10-005.comment: All three are correct. So-called disco accidents happen due to fatigue, physical exhaustion, and being unfit to drive.

2.1.10-101.question_text: What can impair attention in road traffic?

options.text: Strong emotions (e.g., joy, anger, impatience)
Lively conversation
Exciting shows on the car radio

2.1.10-101.comment: Any external stimuli like joy, anger, interesting things on the radio, and lively conversations can negatively affect your attention while driving, as they can be distracting.

2.1.10-102.question_text: What distracts you a lot while driving?

options.text: Talking on the phone
Lighting a cigarette
Whining kids in the backseat

2.1.10-102.comment: Talking on the phone while driving is only allowed with a hands-free system, and it's still a distraction. Lighting a cigarette is also a big distraction since it takes your eyes off the road. Whining kids and passengers can really pull your focus away, so it might be a good idea to take a break.

2.1.11-008.question_text: After following a very slow car on a country road for a long time, you can finally overtake. How do you behave?

options.text: I merge in with enough distance to not hinder the other driver
I briefly slow down to point out their slow driving
I drive noticeably slowly to show the other driver the impact of their behavior

2.1.11-008.comment: In this situation, you should stay calm and overtake with enough safety distance, without endangering anyone. Avoid cutting in closely, as that can lead to accidents.

2.1.11-009-M.question_text: The car in front of you has been preventing you from overtaking for a while. What should you do?

options.text: I wait until I can overtake
I tailgate
I honk and flash my lights several times

2.1.11-009-M.comment: You should wait until it's safe to overtake and always keep a safe distance from the car in front. Stay calm; tailgating, excessive flashing, or honking is considered harassment and can lead to fines or even losing your license.

2.1.11-012.question_text: What do you need to consider when driving after a long workday?

options.text: I drive less focused
I get tired faster
I make fewer driving mistakes

2.1.11-012.comment: After a long workday, you're usually not at your best and get tired more quickly. This can lead to more driving mistakes and decreased concentration.

2.1.11-013.question_text: How can you recognize a good driver?

options.text: They have a calm and relaxed driving style
They don’t react to provocations in traffic
They always point out other drivers' mistakes

2.1.11-013.comment: A good driver always tries to behave cooperatively and understands that people can make mistakes.

2.1.11-014-M.question_text: The red car in front of you has been driving slowly for a while. How should you behave in this situation?

options.text: I maintain my speed
I overtake since the road is clear
I reduce the distance and honk

2.1.11-014-M.comment: You should keep your speed to avoid tailgating and maintain a safe distance. Tailgating, driving too closely, and honking are prohibited in traffic. The road may be clear, but you can only see up to the next curve, which isn't enough for a safe overtaking.

2.1.11-015.question_text: What often causes so-called disco accidents among young drivers?

options.text: A lack of traffic awareness
A high willingness to take risks
A defensive driving style

2.1.11-015.comment: Young drivers often have less experience and a higher willingness to take risks due to wanting to impress others. They may misjudge danger situations, leading to more accidents. A defensive driving style can help avoid accidents.

2.1.11-016.question_text: Why can driving under time pressure be dangerous?

options.text: Dangers are underestimated
Driving too fast
Driving defensively

2.1.11-016.comment: When you're under time pressure, you might underestimate dangers because your willingness to take risks increases, and you often drive too fast. You should still drive defensively and stick to speed limits to keep yourself and others safe.

2.1.11-017.question_text: You're driving on a road outside of town and a car in front of you is going noticeably slower than allowed and possible for them. How should you react?

options.text: I adjust my speed to match the car's
I overtake at a suitable place
I use my horn until the car speeds up

2.1.11-017.comment: Even if it annoys you, you have to adjust your speed to that of the car and not tailgate. Using your horn in this case is considered aggressive and isn't allowed. Overtake only when it's safe to do so, and don't put yourself or others at risk.

2.1.11-018.question_text: Why is frequently changing lanes not a good idea?

options.text: Because it increases the risk of driving errors
Because the time saved is usually very little
Because it can endanger other road users

2.1.11-018.comment: Every time you change lanes, you need to watch traffic, signal, and actually make the change. During this, you might overlook or endanger other road users. Changing lanes often doesn't save much time, and the more you do it, the more likely you are to make mistakes.

2.1.11-118.question_text: A car cuts in front of you after overtaking without enough distance. How do you react?

options.text: I stay calm to avoid conflicts
I slow down to restore the safe distance
I use my horn to alert them to the obstruction

2.1.11-118.comment: The driver in the overtaking vehicle is behaving poorly, but you shouldn't let it unsettle you. Stay calm, don't honk or use your horn. Just slow down a bit to regain the necessary safe distance between the vehicles.

2.1.11-119.question_text: The risk of causing an accident while driving a vehicle is significantly higher between the ages of 18 and 24. What are common causes for this?

options.text: Too little driving experience
Overestimating one's abilities
Increased willingness to take risks

2.1.11-119.comment: Young drivers often lack the experience to properly assess risks on the road. They tend to drive carelessly and take risks, overestimating their abilities and relying on the safety of their vehicles. By testing their cars and their own driving skills, they sometimes find themselves in situations they can't handle.

2.1.11-120.question_text: While you're stuck in traffic, you see in your rearview mirror that a motorcyclist is weaving through the line of waiting cars. How do you react?

options.text: I let them pass
I honk and note their license plate
I make sure they have to stop too

2.1.11-120.comment: You must not act improperly just because another road user is breaking the rules. As a driver, you're not allowed to honk, stop the motorcyclist, or prevent them from passing in this situation.

2.1.11-121.question_text: You're driving on a country road and a car behind you is tailgating. How should you respond?

options.text: I maintain my speed and stay right to allow the car to overtake
I speed up until the car stops tailgating me
I slow down until the car stops tailgating me

2.1.11-121.comment: If you're being tailgated on a country road, stay calm and control your speed at a reasonable pace. Avoid slowing down for no reason to not disrupt traffic flow. But don't let yourself be pressured to speed up either. It's best to let the tailgater pass at the next opportunity.

2.1.11-123.question_text: Five young friends are driving to a leisure event. The mood is lively. What dangers can arise from this?

options.text: - distracted by the traffic
- encouraged to drive riskily
- encouraged to drive more slowly

2.1.11-123.comment: The driver might get caught up in the lively mood and be distracted by the others, overlooking dangers and making driving mistakes. It's a good idea to set rules for behavior among passengers before starting the drive, so the driver doesn't seem like a killjoy or get tempted.

2.1.11-125.question_text: You're about to overtake. What might prevent you from doing so?

options.text: Oncoming traffic
The road layout
The condition of the road

2.1.11-125.comment: A driver can only overtake if they can see that the oncoming lane is clear. In this situation, you can't see oncoming traffic, so you shouldn't overtake.

2.1.11-126.question_text: Before starting your drive, you were annoyed. What effects should you avoid while driving?

options.text: Distraction
Aggressiveness
Caution

2.1.11-126.comment: You should avoid anything that could negatively affect your safe driving. This includes distraction and aggressiveness. If you've been annoyed, you shouldn't get behind the wheel right after.

options.text: They anticipate mistakes from other road users
They avoid driving when tired
They can assert themselves in traffic

2.1.11-127.comment: A responsible driver anticipates mistakes from others and doesn't drive when they're very tired or emotionally unstable. They also don't always insist on their rights and avoid distractions.

2.1.11-128.question_text: What feelings can affect your driving behavior?

options.text: Joy and excitement
Fear and sadness
Anger and rage

2.1.11-128.comment: Strong emotions like anger and rage, fear and sadness, as well as joy and excitement can usually affect how you drive. They can distract you from the road and often lead to risky, aggressive, or overly cautious driving. You should participate in traffic only when you're calm and balanced.

2.1.11-129.question_text: What are signs that you should take a break during your drive?

options.text: Increased yawning
Eyes about to close
Difficulty staying in your lane

2.1.11-129.comment: Short naps can lead to serious accidents. If you're yawning a lot, can't keep your eyes open, or have trouble staying in your lane, you should take a break and rest.

2.1.11-130.question_text: Your passenger wants to discuss something with you while you're driving. How should you behave?

options.text: Focus on my driving
Engage in the discussion

2.1.11-130.comment: You shouldn't let yourself get distracted while driving. If your passenger wants to discuss something, you should pull over and stop the car.

2.1.11-131.question_text: Your passenger points out that you're following too closely. How should you respond?

options.text: I take the passenger's advice seriously
I keep a greater distance
I ignore the passenger's advice

2.1.11-131.comment: You should take safety advice from passengers seriously. Keep a greater distance. In built-up areas, you should maintain a distance of at least three car lengths or about 15 meters. Outside built-up areas, follow the 'two-second rule'.

2.1.11-132.question_text: At a red light in the city, another driver is clearly trying to provoke you into a street race. How should you react?

options.text: I ignore this behavior
I accept the challenge but don't exceed 50 km/h
I get out and confront the driver

2.1.11-132.comment: Don't let yourself be provoked and stay calm. Since street racing is generally prohibited, you should ignore this behavior.

2.1.11-133.question_text: What cause often leads to so-called disco accidents among young drivers?

options.text: Little driving experience in the dark
Lack of experience with fully loaded vehicles
Distractions from passengers

2.1.11-133.comment: Young drivers often have less experience driving at night with full vehicles. Additionally, the risk of accidents increases due to distracting passengers.

2.2.02-006.question_text: You're driving on a road outside the city with three marked lanes in each direction. On the right lane, there are some slower vehicles spaced out. Which lane can you drive continuously?

options.text: The middle
The left

2.2.02-006.comment: You can only use the left lane for short overtaking of other vehicles. You can drive continuously in the middle lane if the road is outside built-up areas and has a guiding line, even if there are only a few vehicles in the right lane.

2.2.02-101-M.question_text: How should you behave correctly in this one-way street now?

options.text: I wait until the work allows me to continue
I turn around and go back
I drive in reverse

2.2.02-101-M.comment: You should only continue when the work allows it. In a one-way street, you can only drive in one direction. So you can't turn around or drive in reverse. You're responsible for any potential accidents.

2.2.03-006.question_text: You're driving at 100 km/h, have a 1-second reaction time, and perform a normal brake. How long is the stopping distance according to the rule of thumb?
2.2.03-006.comment: The stopping distance during normal braking is made up of the reaction distance ((speed : 10) x 3) and the braking distance (speed : 10) x (speed : 10). Stopping distance = reaction distance + braking distance. So at a speed of 100 km/h, the stopping distance is 130 meters.

2.2.03-007.question_text: You're driving at 100 km/h and perform a normal brake. How long is the braking distance according to the rule of thumb?
2.2.03-007.comment: Braking distance = (speed : 10) x (speed : 10). So at a speed of 100 km/h, the braking distance is 100 meters.

2.2.03-008.question_text: You're driving at 100 km/h and have a reaction time of 1 second. How long is the reaction distance according to the rule of thumb?
2.2.03-008.comment: Reaction distance = (speed ÷ 10) x 3. So at a speed of 100 km/h, the reaction distance is 30 meters.

2.2.03-009.question_text: You're driving at 50 km/h, have a reaction time of 1 second, and are making a normal brake. How long is the stopping distance according to the rule of thumb?
2.2.03-009.comment: The stopping distance during a normal brake is the sum of the reaction distance ((speed ÷ 10) x 3) and the braking distance (speed ÷ 10) x (speed ÷ 10). Stopping distance = reaction distance + braking distance. So at a speed of 50 km/h, the stopping distance is 40 meters.

2.2.03-010.question_text: You're driving at 50 km/h and making a normal brake. How long is the braking distance according to the rule of thumb?
2.2.03-010.comment: Braking distance = (speed ÷ 10) x (speed ÷ 10). So at a speed of 50 km/h, the braking distance is 25 meters.

2.2.03-011.question_text: You're driving at 50 km/h and have a reaction time of 1 second. How long is the reaction distance according to the rule of thumb?
2.2.03-011.comment: Reaction distance = (speed ÷ 10) x 3. So at a speed of 50 km/h, the reaction distance is 15 meters.

2.2.03-012.question_text: You're driving on a very narrow road and have 50 m visibility. What should your stopping distance be at most?
2.2.03-012.comment: On a narrow road, you need to be able to stop within half of your visibility, since oncoming traffic also needs to stop in time.

2.2.03-015.question_text: What's the rule of thumb to calculate the braking distance for an emergency brake on a flat, dry, asphalt road?

options.text: (speed in km/h ÷ 10 x speed in km/h ÷ 10) ÷ 2
(speed in km/h ÷ 10 x 5) ÷ 2
(speed in km/h ÷ 10 x 3) ÷ 2

2.2.03-015.comment: (speed in km/h ÷ 10 x speed in km/h ÷ 10) ÷ 2. This is the correct formula to calculate the braking distance for an emergency brake. You take the braking distance formula and divide the result by 2 for emergency braking.

2.2.03-016.question_text: You're driving at 40 km/h. In an emergency brake, the braking distance is about 8 meters. How long is the braking distance under the same conditions at 50 km/h?
2.2.03-016.comment: You calculate the normal braking distance of your vehicle using this rule of thumb: speed divided by 10 times speed divided by 10. For an emergency brake, you take that value and divide it by 2. So for 50 km/h: 50 ÷ 10 * 50 ÷ 10 = 25, divided by 2 = 12.5 meters.

2.2.03-018.question_text: How fast can you drive with a car and a trailer outside built-up areas at most?
2.2.03-018.comment: When towing a trailer with a car, you can drive a maximum of 80 km/h outside built-up areas.

2.2.03-024.question_text: You're driving at night on a well-built country road using your low beam headlights. How far can you stop within?

options.text: Low beam
High beam
Parking light

2.2.03-024.comment: You need to be able to stop within the range of your low beam headlights because the parking light is too weak to provide any visible illumination. If you rely on the high beam range to stop, you risk a collision.

2.2.03-025.question_text: You're driving on the highway in fog with visibility of less than 50 meters. What's the maximum speed you can drive?
2.2.03-025.comment:
You can only drive as fast as you can stop within your visibility range. At 50 km/h, your stopping distance is about 40 meters. So, you shouldn't drive faster than 50 km/h. 

Stopping distance = reaction distance + braking distance 
(Speed in km/h : 10) x 3 + (Speed in km/h : 10) x (Speed in km/h : 10)

2.2.03-101.question_text: What's the maximum speed for a vehicle with snow chains?
2.2.03-101.comment: With snow chains, the maximum speed is 50 km/h. Exceeding this speed can affect driving stability and damage the road.

2.2.03-104.question_text: What's the maximum speed you can drive with a car outside built-up areas on roads with one lane in each direction?
2.2.03-104.comment: For vehicles up to 3.5 tons total weight and without a trailer, the maximum speed is 100 km/h.

2.2.03-305.question_text: On which roads does the recommended speed of 130 km/h apply?

options.text: On highways
On roads outside built-up areas with physically separated lanes for each direction
On roads outside built-up areas with at least two marked lanes for each direction

2.2.03-305.comment: The recommended speed of 130 km/h applies on highways and on roads outside built-up areas with physically separated lanes. You still need to keep enough distance to stop in time.

2.2.04-001.question_text: You're driving at 80 km/h behind another car. What's the minimum safe distance you should keep?

options.text: A 'two-second distance'
A 'one-second distance'
A distance of 15 meters

2.2.04-001.comment: When following another vehicle, you need to maintain the 'two-second distance' or 'half-speed distance' to be able to stop in time. At 80 km/h, this is about 40 meters.

2.2.04-002.question_text: You're driving in city traffic on a dry road in a line of cars moving at 50 km/h. What's the minimum safe distance you should keep from the car in front?

options.text: 15 m, about 3 car lengths
10 m, about 2 car lengths
5 m, about 1 car length

2.2.04-002.comment: In urban areas, shorter distances are acceptable compared to outside built-up areas. The general 'two-second distance' can be reduced to one second with attentive driving and good road conditions, which is about 15 meters at 50 km/h. That's roughly three car lengths.

2.2.04-004.question_text: What minimum safety distance should you keep from the vehicle in front of you when driving at 100 km/h?
2.2.04-004.comment: To be able to brake in time, you should keep half your speed in meters as your distance.

2.2.04-102.question_text: When must a car with a trailer maintain such a distance from the vehicle in front on roads outside built-up areas that a vehicle overtaking can merge in?
2.2.04-102.comment: According to StVO § 4 Abs. 2: "Motor vehicles subject to a special speed limit, as well as trains longer than 7 m, must maintain a distance from the vehicle in front outside built-up areas that allows an overtaking vehicle to merge in."

2.2.04-105-M.question_text: You're driving a car with a trailer. What applies to the distance from the vehicle in front?

options.text: - is appropriate because the overtaking car can merge in front of me
- must be restored after the overtaking car merges in
- is too large because it exceeds the length of my vehicle combination by a lot

2.2.04-105-M.comment: The distance to the vehicle in front should generally be large enough for an overtaking vehicle to merge in. After it merges, you should adjust your distance again, as it shouldn't be larger than your vehicle combination's length.

2.2.04-106.question_text: You're driving a heavily loaded car. Why should you keep a larger safety distance from the vehicles in front?

options.text: - it can increase the braking distance
- it can change the car's handling
- it can extend my reaction time

2.2.04-106.comment: The extra weight changes how the car handles. The brakes are under more stress, which can reduce braking performance and increase the braking distance.

2.2.04-107.question_text: From what length of a vehicle combination do you need to maintain such a distance from the vehicle in front outside built-up areas that an overtaking vehicle can merge in?
2.2.04-107.comment: If the length of your vehicle combination is more than 7 meters, you need to keep a larger distance from the vehicle in front outside built-up areas. This allows overtaking vehicles to merge in front of you.

2.2.05-005.question_text: You're driving at 100 km/h on a road outside built-up areas. In front of you, a truck is going 70 km/h. How far must you be from the hilltop at the start of an overtaking maneuver?
2.2.05-005.comment: The rough formula for the overtaking distance is based on speeds, overtaking time, and vehicle lengths. The values are (1) car speed: 100 km/h (2) truck speed: 70 km/h (3) safety distance before overtaking: half the speed of the car - 50m (4) car length - 4.5m (5) safety distance after overtaking: half the speed of the truck - 35m (6) truck length - 16m. Adding these gives L=105.5m. The formula is: s = (V1 / (V1-V2)) * L. V1 is the car speed and V2 is the truck speed. The calculation is: s = (100 km/h / (100 km/h - 70 km/h)) * 105.5m. s = 352m. On unclear roads, this value should be doubled for safety, resulting in s = 704m. Due to variations in lengths and distances, an overtaking distance of 800 meters should be considered.

2.2.05-011.question_text: How should you behave in this situation?

options.text: I stop the overtaking maneuver and merge to the right
I accelerate and continue the overtaking maneuver
I continue the overtaking maneuver at the same speed

2.2.05-011.comment: You can drive on the opposite lane if you intend to overtake. However, you must increase your speed beyond the allowed 130 km/h, which isn't allowed in this situation. You need to stop the overtaking maneuver and merge to the right.

2.2.05-012.question_text: What should you be prepared for now?

options.text: - blue cars starting to overtake
- the overtaking maneuver of the green truck taking longer
- white trucks accelerating

2.2.05-012.comment: You should be prepared that you might not be able to overtake now because other nearby traffic participants are already involved in overtaking maneuvers. Don't act hastily just to finish the overtaking within a permissible distance. A solid line means no overtaking and is equivalent to the traffic sign "No Overtaking."

2.2.05-013.question_text: Who should you pay special attention to in this situation?

options.text: - cyclists
- the red car
- the white truck

2.2.05-013.comment: In this situation, you need to pay attention to the cyclist approaching from your right. The cyclist might ride onto the road in front of the truck, creating a dangerous situation.

2.2.05-014-M.question_text: Why do you need to slow down now?

options.text: - motorcycle
- tractor
- off-road vehicle

2.2.05-014-M.comment: The overtaking motorcyclist poses a danger to you. They're coming towards you in your lane while overtaking. You should slow down to avoid a collision. The behavior of the other drivers is in line with traffic rules.

2.2.05-016-M.question_text: You want to overtake. How should you behave now?

options.text: I won't overtake yet, as the blue car might be overtaking
I follow the blue car closely if it overtakes
I overtake all vehicles in one go

2.2.05-016-M.comment: You need to wait to overtake until the vehicle in front of you has finished overtaking. A solid line (no overtaking line) and a no overtaking sign indicate that overtaking is not allowed. A broken line (guiding line) means overtaking is allowed.

2.2.05-017.question_text: How should you behave correctly now?

options.text: - not
- right
- left

2.2.05-017.comment: Plan your overtaking so that you finish before the solid line, also known as the no overtaking line, begins. A solid line means, just like the corresponding traffic sign, that overtaking is prohibited.

2.2.05-018.question_text: You want to overtake a truck with a trailer. What do you need to consider?

options.text: The required overtaking distance is significantly longer due to the trailer
The outline of the truck can hide vehicles in front
You can only start to overtake directly behind the truck

2.2.05-018.comment: When you want to overtake a truck with a trailer, you should factor in that the required overtaking distance is longer because of the trailer, and that the outline of the truck might hide vehicles ahead.

2.2.05-019.question_text: Why can't you overtake the bus in front of you right now?

options.text: Because of the warning lights on the bus
Because of the motorcycle
Because of the missing road markings

2.2.05-019.comment: The bus has its warning lights on and is still approaching the bus stop. In this case, it's not allowed to overtake the bus. Also, the motorcycle behind you is getting ready to overtake.

2.2.05-103-M.question_text: What could make this situation dangerous?

options.text: Due to oncoming traffic
Due to the red car
Due to the tractor

2.2.05-103-M.comment: The driver approaching from behind is trying to overtake you before the curve, even though they can't see around it. If oncoming traffic is approaching in this situation, both it and the car driver could become dangerous due to their evasive maneuvers. The tractor next to the road is not a danger.

2.2.06-101-M.question_text: How should you behave correctly here?

options.text: I slow down and wait
I line up on the right behind the already waiting vehicles
I continue at a reduced speed

2.2.06-101-M.comment: The distance to the cyclist isn't enough. Stop and wait until they pass through the narrow spot. This way, you can ensure you don't endanger the cyclist.

2.2.07-002.question_text: Which motor vehicles have free lane choice in built-up areas?
2.2.07-002.comment: In Germany, there's a rule to drive on the right. Motor vehicles up to 3.5 tons total weight are exempt from this rule in built-up areas and can choose their lane freely.

2.2.07-005.question_text: What could create a dangerous situation?

options.text: - yellow trucks
- green trucks
- vehicles in front

2.2.07-005.comment: The fast driving style of the yellow truck suggests it might also overtake the blue truck in front of it. Your speed is faster than that of the trucks. You can't swerve left because a car is directly behind you in the left lane. If the yellow truck swerves out, you’ll have to brake hard.

options.text: I stay in the middle lane and slow down
I switch to the right lane and slow down
I switch to the left lane and overtake the red car in front of me

2.2.07-007.comment: Stay in the middle lane and slow down. The car ahead will also slow down soon to let the car in the left lane merge, as that lane is ending. You can't switch left, and switching to the right lane would also be too dangerous.

options.text: I reduce my speed
I continue at the same speed
I merge into the right lane

2.2.07-008.comment: You're in the middle lane and need to stay there while reducing your speed. The driver in the left lane is going slower. You can't overtake them on the right. You also can't switch to the right lane because there's a vehicle there.

2.2.07-009.question_text: What should you expect in this situation?

options.text: - a gray car will switch to the middle lane
- a yellow truck will pull out to overtake in front of me
- a gray car will stay in the right lane

2.2.07-009.comment: Since the vehicle is merging onto the highway quickly from the right, you should expect it to switch to the middle lane. This impression is strengthened by the trucks maintaining their speed and distance.

options.text: I reduce my speed and stay in the middle lane
I maintain my speed and stay in the middle lane
I maintain my speed and switch to the right lane

2.2.07-010.comment: A car is in front of you, and another car is merging onto the main highway from the right. It's clear that the car in the left lane is going slower than you. Since overtaking can only happen on the left, you need to slow down and reduce your speed.

2.2.07-011.question_text: When should the zipper merge method be used on a road with multiple marked lanes in one direction?

options.text: When a lane ends
When a lane is not fully drivable due to an obstacle
When a merging lane ends on the highway

2.2.07-011.comment: The zipper merge method should be used when a lane cannot be driven on any longer. The exception is the highway.

2.2.07-012-M.question_text: What applies to the use of the shoulder in this situation?

options.text: - must be used like a right lane
- may only be used in case of a breakdown
- may only be used by trucks

2.2.07-012-M.comment: The traffic sign indicates that the shoulder should be used like the right lane.

2.2.07-013-M.question_text: What applies to the use of the shoulder in this situation?

options.text: - may only be used in case of a breakdown
- may only be used by trucks
- must be used like a right lane

2.2.07-013-M.comment: The shoulder should not be used regularly. You can only use it in case of a breakdown.

2.2.09-002-M.question_text: Why do you have to wait before turning left?

options.text: - motorcycles
- cars
- bicycles

2.2.09-002-M.comment: As a left turner, you generally have to give way to all traffic coming from your direction or approaching you from the left. This includes cyclists, pedestrians, motorcyclists, etc.

options.text: - turn left after the red vehicle has passed me
- turn left now to clear the road
- turn left now to avoid confusing those behind me with my hesitation

2.2.09-003-M.comment: If you want to turn left and a car is trying to overtake you from the left, you need to let it pass first. Only after the car has finished overtaking can you turn.

2.2.09-004-M.question_text: You want to turn left. How should you behave correctly?

options.text: I stop at the field path and wait
I speed up and turn quickly
I keep going because I can't turn here

2.2.09-004-M.comment: The motorcycle rider behind you (in the left lane) is already very close. Please stop at the field path and wait until you can turn.

2.2.09-101.question_text: How should you behave correctly when reversing?

options.text: - check the area around you with a full look
- drive attentively and slowly
- make sure there are no people in the blind spot

2.2.09-101.comment: When reversing, look behind you and check the area around you with a full look, drive attentively and slowly, and make sure there are no people in your blind spot for safety.

options.text: On highways and main roads outside of parking areas
In sharp curves
At bus stops

2.2.12-001.comment: In general, the traffic regulations prohibit stopping in places where it could be dangerous for other road users or threaten public safety. This especially applies to stopping on highways or main roads, as well as in sharp and blind curves.

options.text: On narrow roads opposite driveways
At taxi stands
Immediately behind pedestrian crossings

2.2.12-003.comment: Parking is prohibited where it can obstruct other road users or compromise public order and safety. This includes taxi stands, narrow roads, and driveways, as well as on and up to 5 meters before pedestrian crossings.

2.2.12-102.question_text: Up to what total permissible weight can vehicles be parked on specially marked sidewalks?
2.2.12-102.comment: Vehicles with a total permissible weight of up to 2.8 tons can park on specially marked sidewalks.

2.2.12-104.question_text: What minimum distance from a traffic light must a vehicle maintain when stopping if it would be obscured by the vehicle?
2.2.12-104.comment: You must maintain a minimum distance of 10 meters so that the traffic signals are not obscured.

2.2.12-105.question_text: Where can you regularly park a trailer with a permissible total weight of more than 2 tons in urban areas on Sundays and public holidays, as well as between 10 PM and 6 AM?

options.text: In commercial areas
In residential areas in appropriately marked parking spaces
In special areas designated for recreation, on sufficiently wide streets

2.2.12-105.comment: Parking a trailer with a permissible total weight of more than 2 tons is allowed in commercial and residential areas with appropriately marked parking spaces. Regular parking is prohibited in urban areas and in special recreational areas from 10 PM to 6 AM, as well as on Sundays and public holidays.

2.2.12-106.question_text: What should you pay attention to when parking a trailer without a towing vehicle?

options.text: - may not be parked on public roads for more than 2 weeks
- may be parked in appropriately marked parking spaces for more than 2 weeks
- may be parked on sufficiently paved shoulders indefinitely

2.2.12-106.comment: Note that you cannot park trailers without a towing vehicle on regular parking spaces for more than two weeks. The same applies to paved shoulders. However, this rule does not apply to appropriately marked parking spaces.

2.2.12-107-M.question_text: You want to park at the right side of the road. How should you behave in this situation?

options.text: I give up the parking space, even though I have the right of way
I park now because I have the right of way

2.2.12-107-M.comment: You signaled first, so you have the right of way for the parking space. To avoid a conflict, you should still give up the parking space.

2.2.12-108-M.question_text: You're about to park on the right side of the road. Who has the right of way in this situation?

options.text: The blue car has the right of way
I have the right of way
Neither has the right of way, we need to communicate

2.2.12-108-M.comment: The car in front of you signaled first, so it has the right of way in the parking area. If you try to park now, you could collide with it.

2.2.12-203.question_text: Which signs do you need to keep at least 10 meters away from if they would be blocked by your vehicle?

options.text: Railroad crossing sign
Stop. Yield right of way.
No stopping sign

2.2.12-203.comment: You need to keep at least 10 meters away from signs like the railroad crossing, traffic lights, or the 'Stop! Yield right of way' sign, especially if your vehicle would block them. You can stop at a stop sign, but stopping behind it is not allowed.

2.2.12-204.question_text: You're about to park on the right side of the road. How far must you be from the solid lane marking at a minimum?
2.2.12-204.comment: When parking, you need to keep at least 3 meters away from the lane marking to ensure that your parked car doesn't become an obstacle.

2.2.13-001.question_text: Where do you need to use a parking disc to park?

options.text: At a broken parking meter
Where required by traffic signs
In a restricted no stopping area

2.2.13-001.comment: You must use a parking disc wherever traffic signs require it. You also need one if a broken parking meter makes it impossible to get a valid parking ticket. Using a parking disc in a restricted no stopping area doesn't allow you to park there for more than three minutes.

2.2.13-002.question_text: A parking meter hasn't expired yet. What should you do?

options.text: - take advantage of it without using the meter again
- not take advantage of it
- only take advantage of it if you use a parking disc

2.2.13-002.comment: If a parking meter hasn't expired yet, you can use the remaining parking time and park your vehicle there for free. You don't need a parking disc for this.

2.2.13-003.question_text: You arrive at 10:40 AM in an area where you can park for 2 hours with a parking disc. What time do you need to set on the parking disc?
